<!-- file: README.md -->

# freetoken-rdna3

![freetoken-rdna3: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on RX 7900 XTX / XT, NVFP4 and EXL3 checkpoints](docs/rdna3/assets/social-preview.png)

**Run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model, on your own PC with one or two AMD Radeon RX 7900
XTX / XT cards.** You get a local server with an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API: chat apps, coding agents
(OpenCode, Claude Code) and your own scripts use it like a cloud API, with 262k tokens of context per conversation (up
to 1M with `xtx-xt-1m`), while the model runs on your hardware.

It is a tuned build of the [FreeToken](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken) MoE engine for RDNA3 (ROCm). The model
does not fit in VRAM: every expert lives in system RAM and the GPUs keep the most used ones; two unequal cards share
the work.

## What you need

| | |
|---|---|
| GPUs | one or two RX 7900 XTX (24 GB) / RX 7900 XT (20 GB); other cards: [which GPUs](docs/rdna3/limits.md#which-gpus) |
| RAM | 128 GB recommended: the server locks ~52 to ~83 GiB, depending on the checkpoint and the number of cards ([table](#which-checkpoint)), more with conversations kept in RAM, and the system and your programs need ~30 GiB beside it ([how to count](docs/rdna3/limits.md#how-much-ram-do-i-need)) |
| Disk | 85 to 135 GB for the model, ~27 GB for the image (~29 GB more while it builds) |
| System | Linux x86_64 with the in-kernel `amdgpu` driver, and Docker. ROCm, PyTorch and the rest come inside the image |

`rdna3/serve.sh --check` looks at your machine, says what is missing, which profile fits your GPUs and what fits in your
RAM. It changes nothing.

## Quick start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Cedriceuh/freetoken-rdna3 && cd freetoken-rdna3
rdna3/serve.sh --check                                   # what this machine has, which profile fits (no image yet: expected)
docker build -f Dockerfile.rdna3 -t freetoken-rdna3:latest .    # once; pulls a 25 GB ROCm base image
rdna3/download.sh nvfp4                                  # 135 GB into ~/models (or exl3-3.05, exl3-4.05: see below)
rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4  # use the profile --check suggests
```

The server loads in ~2.5 minutes on the reference machine (the first start of a new image also compiles GPU kernels for
a few minutes). It is
ready when `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1919/health` answers `"ok"`. Then, from another terminal:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "qwen3.8-flash-next", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello! Who are you?"}],
  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}}'
```

Every step explained, with client set-ups and running it as a service:
[docs/rdna3/getting-started.md](docs/rdna3/getting-started.md).

## What you can do with it

- **Chat** from any app that speaks the OpenAI API: base URL `http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1`, model `qwen3.8-flash-next`,
  any API key.
- **Run coding agents**: OpenCode through the OpenAI API (the client every agent measurement here used), or a client
  of the Anthropic API such as Claude Code (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1919`; not measured here). Tool calls
  and thinking are supported. On two cards up to four
  requests run at once, so sub-agents work in parallel. Set-ups:
  [connect a client](docs/rdna3/getting-started.md#7-connect-a-client).
- **Work on long inputs**: 262,144 tokens per conversation on two cards, 131,072 on one. With the attention K/V moved
  to RAM, `xtx-xt-4x262k` holds four such conversations at once (three with NVFP4 on 128 GB) and `xtx-xt-1m` one of up to 1M
  tokens; each 262k
  conversation then takes 6.9 GiB of RAM ([long context](docs/rdna3/long-context.md), `rdna3/serve.sh --check`).
- **Switch between conversations**: one pushed off the GPUs is kept in system RAM and resumes in ~2 s instead of being
  read again.
- **Send images** with `rdna3/serve.sh ... --vision` ([images](docs/rdna3/limits.md#images-vision)).
- **Script it** with any OpenAI or Anthropic SDK, or serve your network (`--host 0.0.0.0`, add an API key:
  [security](docs/rdna3/limits.md#anything-else-to-know)).

## Which profile?

A profile holds every setting for one GPU setup; `rdna3/serve.sh <profile>` picks the cards by itself.

| Your GPUs | Profile | Context | Requests at once | Status |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| RX 7900 XTX + RX 7900 XT | `xtx-xt` | 262k, shared by the requests | 4 | measured |
| the same, several agents with long conversations (K/V in RAM) | `xtx-xt-4x262k` | 262k each | up to 4, as your RAM allows | measured |
| the same, one conversation past 262k (K/V in RAM) | `xtx-xt-1m` | 1M | 4, sharing 1M | measured with EXL3 3.05 bpw |
| two RX 7900 XTX | `xtx-xtx` | 262k | 4 | untested; EXL3 needs `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.6` |
| two RX 7900 XT | `xt-xt` | 262k | 4 | untested; EXL3 needs `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.6` |
| one RX 7900 XTX | `xtx` | 131k | 1 | measured |
| one RX 7900 XT | `xt` | 131k | 1 | measured |
| one RX 7900 GRE | `gre` | 65k | 1 | untested |

Untested profiles are derived from the measured ones; the script says so when you start one. Measured one? Please open
an issue with your numbers. Details and adapting a profile to other cards: [profiles](docs/rdna3/profiles.md).

## Which checkpoint?

All three run on `xtx-xt`, `xtx` and `xt` with nothing to change: download one and point `--model` at its directory.
`xtx-xt-1m` is measured with EXL3 3.05 bpw only, `xtx-xt-4x262k` with EXL3 3.05 bpw (four conversations) and NVFP4
(three) ([profiles](docs/rdna3/profiles.md#xtx-xt-4x262k-and-xtx-xt-1m-the-kv-in-host-ram)). "bpw" is bits per weight;
the other terms: [glossary](docs/rdna3/README.md#terms-used-in-these-pages).

| | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `rdna3/download.sh` | `nvfp4` | `exl3-3.05` | `exl3-4.05` |
| Hugging Face | [RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) | [turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3](https://huggingface.co/turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3) | [turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3](https://huggingface.co/turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3) |
| Download | 135 GB | 85 GB | 108 GB |
| RAM locked: two cards; one card | ~83 GiB; ~74 GiB | ~61 GiB; ~52 GiB | ~76 GiB; ~67 GiB |

EXL3 3.05 bpw is the smallest and decodes the fastest on every measured profile ([speed](#speed)): its experts are smaller, so more of
them stay in VRAM (the checkpoints also differ in how many of the MTP head's drafts are kept). On the
maintainers' agentic benchmark (29 planted bugs to fix in long agent sessions, on an earlier build) NVFP4 fixed 12 and
18 in two runs, EXL3 3.05 bpw 13 and 4.05 bpw 12 in one run each: too few runs to rank them.

## Speed

One request, greedy, the model's MTP draft head on (as the profiles ship): one conversation grown from 9k tokens to the
profile's maximum context with blocks the server has never seen, like large tool results
([method](docs/rdna3/benchmarks.md#how-the-numbers-are-taken)).

| Decode (TG) | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `xtx-xt`: RX 7900 XTX + XT, 9k to 260k tokens | 78-96 tok/s | 95-117 tok/s | 86-94 tok/s |
| `xtx`: one RX 7900 XTX, 9k to 124k tokens | 36-44 tok/s | 52-58 tok/s | 37-47 tok/s |
| `xt`: one RX 7900 XT, 9k to 124k tokens | 29-34 tok/s | 41-46 tok/s | 29-36 tok/s |

| Reading a new 6-52k-token block (PP); agent turn, time to first token | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `xtx-xt`, 9k to 260k tokens | 1910-2180 tok/s; 0.8-0.9 s | 1940-2280 tok/s; 0.7-0.9 s | 1970-2270 tok/s; 0.8-1.0 s |
| `xtx`, 9k to 124k tokens | 1520-1670 tok/s; 1.5-1.6 s | 1700-1820 tok/s; 1.0-1.2 s | 1640-1820 tok/s; 1.3-1.5 s |
| `xt`, 9k to 124k tokens | 1350-1480 tok/s; 1.6-1.8 s | 1500-1600 tok/s; 1.2-1.3 s | 1450-1620 tok/s; 1.5-1.6 s |

An "agent turn" is ~1k new tokens (a tool result) added to a conversation the server already holds (that column comes
from an earlier build, before the latest short-prefill changes).
Requests running at once share the GPUs: on `xtx-xt-4x262k`, four agents at 257-260k tokens decode at 29.6-31.6 tok/s
each, one alone at 95.1 (EXL3 3.05 bpw, one pass on an earlier build than the tables above). All the numbers:
[benchmarks](docs/rdna3/benchmarks.md).

## Status

Tested on one machine: RX 7900 XTX + RX 7900 XT (gfx1100), Threadripper 3970X, 128 GB DDR4, ROCm 10.1 in the
container. Other RDNA3 cards, RDNA4, more than two GPUs and NVIDIA are untested ([limits](docs/rdna3/limits.md)).
Reports from other setups are very welcome.

## Credits and license

A modified version of [FreeToken](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken) (Apache License 2.0), with ROCm work from
the FreeToken community. What changed from upstream and who wrote what: [NOTICE](NOTICE),
[docs/rdna3/changes-from-upstream.md](docs/rdna3/changes-from-upstream.md), [docs/rdna3/credits.md](docs/rdna3/credits.md).

# freetoken-rdna3 documentation

New here? Start with [getting-started.md](getting-started.md): from a Linux machine to a running server and your tools
connected to it.

| I want to | Page |
|---|---|
| install it, run it, connect a client, run it as a service, update it | [getting-started.md](getting-started.md) |
| fix something that goes wrong, report a bug | [troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md) |
| know if my RAM, GPUs or model will work (FAQ) | [limits.md](limits.md) |
| understand or adapt a hardware profile | [profiles.md](profiles.md) |
| serve four 262k conversations at once, or one of 1M | [long-context.md](long-context.md) |
| let the CPU compute part of the experts (`--hybrid`, off by default) | [cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md) |
| look up an environment variable this build adds | [options.md](options.md) |
| see the measurements and how they were taken | [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md) |
| understand what changed in the engine, and why | [how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md) |
| know what was tried and dropped (dated history) | [journey.md](journey.md) |
| check a change, report numbers | [testing.md](testing.md) |
| sync with upstream, release | [maintaining.md](maintaining.md), [changes-from-upstream.md](changes-from-upstream.md) |
| see who wrote what | [credits.md](credits.md) |

Upstream FreeToken's own documentation is in the parent directory ([install](../install.md), [CLI](../cli.md),
[models](../models.md), [quickstart](../quickstart.md)); its install guides are not how this build is installed: use
[getting-started.md](getting-started.md).

## Terms used in these pages

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| profile | one file in `rdna3/profiles/` with every setting for one GPU setup (`xtx-xt`, `xtx`, ...) |
| checkpoint | one quantized version of the model's weights: NVFP4, EXL3 3.05 bpw or EXL3 4.05 bpw |
| TP | tensor parallelism: every layer split over the GPUs, which work on every token together |
| TG / decode | generating tokens, in tokens/s |
| PP / prefill | reading the prompt (prompt processing), in tokens/s or as time to first token |
| agent turn | a short new message (a tool result) added to a conversation the server already holds; measured as time to first token |
| MoE, experts | Mixture of Experts: each layer holds 512 small networks, and a router sends each token to 10 of them (plus one shared expert) |
| expert cache | the VRAM left after the other weights and the K/V, filled with the most used experts; the others are copied from RAM when needed (a miss) |
| GDN | GatedDeltaNet, the linear-attention layers (36 of the model's 48) with a fixed-size recurrent state |
| QSA | the model's full-attention layers (12 of 48), which keep a KV cache |
| KV cache, K/V | the attention layers' keys and values for every token of a conversation |
| PLE | per-layer n-gram embeddings: big lookup tables (51 GB; 33 GB in EXL3 3.05 bpw) read from disk |
| NVFP4 | 4-bit floating-point weights with shared scales, the experts' format in the RadixArk checkpoint |
| EXL3 | exllamav3's trellis format (3 or 4 bits per weight here), read by this build for its EXL3 checkpoints ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)) |
| MTP | multi-token prediction, the model's speculative-decoding head: it drafts tokens that one step checks (on in the profiles, `rdna3/serve.sh --no-mtp` turns it off: [options.md](options.md#speculative-decoding-with-the-mtp-head-qwen38-flash-next)) |
| greedy | decoding that always takes the most likely token (temperature 0): a request alone gives the same answer to the same prompt, which is how exactness is checked |
| bit-exact | a change that gives the same greedy answers as without it |
| agentic benchmark | the maintainers' private test: 29 planted bugs an agent must fix in long sessions; the reference for changes that are not bit-exact |
| LDS | the GPU's on-chip shared memory (64 KiB per work group on RDNA3) |
| FTW | FreeToken's own weight format |
| RAM tier | this build's copy of evicted conversations in system RAM (`FREETOKEN_HOST_KV`) |

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

From a Linux machine with one or two RX 7900 cards to a running server and your tools connected to it. Each step says
how to check that it worked. The two downloads (a 25 GB base image, an 85-135 GB model) take most of the time.

## 1. Check your machine

| | Two cards (`xtx-xt`) | One card (`xtx` or `xt`) |
|---|---|---|
| GPUs | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB + RX 7900 XT 20 GB | one RX 7900 XTX 24 GB or RX 7900 XT 20 GB |
| System RAM the server locks: NVFP4; EXL3 3.05 / 4.05 bpw (keep ~30 GiB more for the system) | ~83 GiB; ~61 / ~76 GiB: a **128 GB** machine | ~74 GiB; ~52 / ~67 GiB |
| Disk | 135 GB for the NVFP4 model (85 / 108 GB in EXL3 3.05 / 4.05 bpw), ~27 GB for the image, ~29 GB more while building | same |
| Software | Linux x86_64 with the in-kernel `amdgpu` driver (`/dev/kfd` present), Docker | same |
| Tested on | Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, kernel 7.0 (older kernels untested) | same |

Other setups (two XTX, two XT, a GRE) have untested profiles. How to count the RAM you need, other GPUs and other
models: [limits.md](limits.md#how-much-ram-do-i-need).

The ROCm user space, PyTorch and Triton are inside the image: nothing ROCm-related has to be installed on the host.
Your user must be allowed to run Docker (the `docker` group; log in again after adding it) and be in the `video` and
`render` groups.

Get the code and let the launcher look at the machine:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Cedriceuh/freetoken-rdna3 && cd freetoken-rdna3
rdna3/serve.sh --check
```

It checks the driver, Docker, the image, the GPUs, the RAM each checkpoint needs and the host settings of step 2, and
prints `ok`, `warn` or `FAIL` for each, with the command that fixes it. It names the profile for your GPUs
(`suggested:`), says what fits in your RAM, ends with the command to start the server (`Next:`), and changes nothing. Run it again after each step; with `--model DIR` it also checks a downloaded checkpoint. The image
is missing until step 3: that `FAIL` is expected now.

## 2. Two host settings

Without them the server works but pauses: both are measured on the reference machine
([why](troubleshooting.md#long-pauses-in-the-middle-of-a-run)). The first one is set once; the second one lasts until
the next reboot.

- **Keep memory compaction off the engine's locked memory.** Otherwise the kernel moves memory the GPUs use and the
  driver stops them for 5-22 s while it does. Persistent:

  ```bash
  printf 'vm.compaction_proactiveness=0\nvm.compact_unevictable_allowed=0\n' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-llm-gpu.conf
  sudo sysctl --system
  ```

- **The `COMPUTE` power profile on each card.** With the default one, the VRAM clock stays low for ~10 s after an idle
  pause, and the first request after it waits that long. Until the next reboot (a tool such as LACT can keep it across
  reboots):

  ```bash
  echo 5 | sudo tee /sys/class/drm/card*/device/pp_power_profile_mode   # 5 = COMPUTE in that file's list
  ```

## 3. Build the image

```bash
docker build -f Dockerfile.rdna3 -t freetoken-rdna3:latest .
```

The first build pulls the ROCm PyTorch base image (25 GB, pinned by digest); after that a rebuild takes a couple of
minutes. Build from a git clone, not from a downloaded archive: the build records the commit it was made from
(`/opt/FreeToken-BUILD-PROVENANCE.txt` in the image, which `serve.sh --check` compares with your checkout) and fails
without `.git`. `--build-arg GPU_ARCH=gfx1100` is the default and the only architecture tested. Do not use
`install.sh` or `scripts/`: they install and build upstream's NVIDIA / CUDA wheels.

## 4. Download the model

### Which checkpoint?

Three quantized versions of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next run on `xtx-xt`, `xtx` and `xt` with nothing else to change (the other
profiles: [which checkpoint](../../README.md#which-checkpoint)).

| | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `rdna3/download.sh` name | `nvfp4` | `exl3-3.05` | `exl3-4.05` |
| Download | 135 GB | 85 GB | 108 GB |
| RAM locked: two cards; one card | ~83 GiB; ~74 GiB | ~61 GiB; ~52 GiB | ~76 GiB; ~67 GiB |
| Decode, `xtx-xt` / `xtx` / `xt` | 78-96 / 36-44 / 29-34 tok/s | 95-117 / 52-58 / 41-46 tok/s | 86-94 / 37-47 / 29-36 tok/s |

EXL3 3.05 bpw is the smallest, needs the least RAM and decodes the fastest on every measured profile (its experts are
smaller, so more stay in VRAM; the checkpoints also differ in how many of the MTP head's drafts are kept). On the
maintainers' agentic benchmark (29 planted bugs to fix in long agent sessions, on an earlier build) the EXL3
checkpoints fixed 13 (3.05 bpw) and 12 (4.05 bpw) of 29, one run each; NVFP4 12 and 18 in two runs: too few runs to
rank them. "bpw" is bits per weight; other terms: [glossary](README.md#terms-used-in-these-pages).

### Download

```bash
rdna3/download.sh nvfp4          # or exl3-3.05, exl3-4.05; prints the directory it fills (below)
```

The directories: `~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, `~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3-3.05bpw`,
`~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3-4.05bpw`. It runs the image's own Hugging Face CLI (nothing to install on the host; the files belong to your user), checks the
disk space first, and skips the files already complete when run again after an interruption. A second argument picks
another directory; `HF_TOKEN`, when set, is passed on. With `hf` installed on the host, the same thing by hand:
`hf download RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --local-dir ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, or
`turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3` with `--revision 3.05bpw_h5_ng5` or `--revision 4.05bpw_h6_ng6`.

What the NVFP4 135 GB hold: 68 GB of experts (loaded into RAM), 51 GB of n-gram embedding tables (read from disk on
demand, they never have to fit in RAM), 16 GB of other weights and the tokenizer.

Check: `rdna3/serve.sh --check --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` names the checkpoint and the RAM it needs.

## 5. Start the server

```bash
rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4       # two cards
rdna3/serve.sh xtx    --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4       # one XTX
rdna3/serve.sh xt     --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4       # one XT
```

Use the profile `serve.sh --check` suggested ([which profile](../../README.md#which-profile)); `rdna3/serve.sh --list`
prints them all. The script picks the cards by itself (for two cards the larger one becomes rank 0) and prints them;
`--gpus 1,0` forces a choice (`rdna3/serve.sh --list-gpus` shows the numbers), `--dry-run` prints the full
`docker run` command instead of running it.

Loading takes about 2.5 minutes on the reference machine (it reads ~68 GB of experts into RAM). The very first start of
a new image also compiles and autotunes GPU kernels for a few more minutes; the results are kept in a Docker volume
(`freetoken-rdna3-kcache-<image id>`), so later starts are fast. The server is ready when the log prints
`API server is ready to serve on 127.0.0.1:1919`, or:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1919/health          # {"status": "ok", ...} once loaded ("loading" before)
```

`serve.sh` stays in the foreground: run the next commands from another terminal. Stop it with Ctrl-C or
`docker stop -t 30 freetoken-rdna3` and let it exit (a clean shutdown takes ~9 s). Do not kill it while it is still
loading: that once left GPU memory held until a reboot
([troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#less-vram-or-a-start-that-never-ends-after-a-server-was-killed-while-starting)).

### Options worth knowing

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--port N`, `--host ADDR` | where the API listens (default `127.0.0.1:1919`). `--host 0.0.0.0` serves your network: the API has no authentication unless started with `-- --api-key KEY` ([security](limits.md#anything-else-to-know)) |
| `--ctx N` | a shorter context than the profile's. Where the K/V lives in VRAM, the room it frees goes to the expert cache; with `xtx-xt-1m` it shrinks the K/V kept in RAM; with `xtx-xt-4x262k` it only caps each conversation (the RAM pool is `--kv-reserve-tokens`) |
| `--vision` | accept images ([limits](limits.md#images-vision)); off by default, no measurable speed cost on two cards, ~1.5-2 % of decode on one |
| `--no-mtp` | turn off the MTP draft head: the head speeds up a request decoding alone (+35 % on `xtx-xt`) and up to four at once on `xtx-xt` and its K/V-in-RAM variants; it costs 3-4 % where more requests decode than it verifies (the other profiles, an earlier build; [limits](limits.md#speculative-decoding-mtp)) |
| `--hybrid` | the CPU computes part of the experts missing from VRAM; off by default, not agent-validated. Measured on an earlier build: NVFP4 +46 % decode on `xtx`, +51 % on `xt`, on `xtx-xt` +2 % for one request and +15 % each with four; EXL3 3.05 bpw +5 % on `xtx`, even on `xtx-xt` ([cpu-experts](cpu-experts.md)) |
| `--served-name ID` | the model id `/v1/models` reports (default `qwen3.8-flash-next`) |
| `--name NAME`, `--image REF`, `--memory SIZE` | container name, image, container RAM limit |
| `-- <flags>` | anything after `--` goes to `ft serve` (upstream's [CLI reference](../cli.md)) |

`rdna3/serve.sh --help` lists them all.

## 6. First request

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "qwen3.8-flash-next",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals."}],
  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false},
  "max_tokens": 1024
}'
```

- **Sampling defaults** for any field the request leaves out: temperature 0.6 (`rdna3/serve.sh` passes
  `--default-temperature 0.6`; the checkpoint's `generation_config.json` says 1.0), top_k 20 and top_p 0.95 from that
  file. Keeping `top_k` at 20 (or anything up to 256) uses the fastest sampler.
- **Thinking** is on by default (the reasoning goes to `reasoning_content`); the request above turns it off with
  `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}`. With thinking on, give `max_tokens` room (several thousand): if
  the budget runs out while the model is still thinking, `content` comes back empty with `finish_reason: "length"`.
- **Tool calls** are parsed (Qwen3 coder format) and returned as OpenAI `tool_calls`.

## 7. Connect a client

Endpoints: OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/models`;
Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages`. The server serves one model and answers whatever model name a request carries.
The API key is not checked (use any string) unless the server was started with `-- --api-key KEY`.

For a coding agent, set its context window to the profile's context (262144 for the two-card profiles and
`xtx-xt-4x262k`, 1000000 for `xtx-xt-1m`, 131072 for `xtx` / `xt`, 65536 for `gre`, or your `--ctx`), so it compacts
the conversation at the right time.

**Any OpenAI-compatible app** (chat UIs, editors, SDKs): base URL `http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1`, model
`qwen3.8-flash-next`, any API key.

**OpenCode**: a provider in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "freetoken": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "freetoken-rdna3",
      "options": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1", "timeout": false, "headerTimeout": false },
      "models": {
        "qwen3.8-flash-next": {
          "name": "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (local)",
          "reasoning": true,
          "limit": { "context": 262144, "output": 32768 },
          "interleaved": { "field": "reasoning_content" }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "model": "freetoken/qwen3.8-flash-next"
}
```

The two timeouts off keep OpenCode waiting through long first reads; `interleaved` gives the model its earlier
reasoning back in the history (field `reasoning_content`). With `--vision`, add `"attachment": true` and `"modalities": {"input": ["text", "image"], "output":
["text"]}` to the model.

**Claude Code** (or an Anthropic SDK; not measured here) adds `/v1/messages` itself:

```bash
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1919 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=local claude
```

**Python**, with the `openai` package:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:1919/v1", api_key="local")
reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3.8-flash-next",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the plot of Hamlet in three sentences."}],
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}},
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

## 8. Day to day

### Watching it

- `docker logs -f freetoken-rdna3`: one `Prefill batch` line per prompt chunk (new vs cached tokens) and a
  `Decode batch` line every few dozen steps (requests running, tokens in context, tokens/s).
- `curl -s localhost:1919/v1/stats`: throughput, cache use, request counts.
- `curl -s 'localhost:1919/v1/requests?since=0'`: the recent requests with their time to first token.

### Running it as a service

Stop the foreground server first (`serve.sh` removes any container named `freetoken-rdna3` before it starts). A systemd
user unit, `~/.config/systemd/user/freetoken-rdna3.service` (adjust the two paths to where you cloned the repository
and downloaded the model):

```ini
[Unit]
Description=freetoken-rdna3 (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next)

[Service]
# at boot the user manager can start before the Docker daemon: wait for it
ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'until docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
ExecStart=%h/freetoken-rdna3/rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt --model %h/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4
ExecStop=/usr/bin/env docker stop -t 30 freetoken-rdna3
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=15
TimeoutStartSec=300
TimeoutStopSec=60

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

```bash
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user enable --now freetoken-rdna3
loginctl enable-linger "$USER"      # keep it running when you are logged out
```

### Updating

```bash
git pull
docker tag freetoken-rdna3:latest freetoken-rdna3:prev     # keep the current image to go back to
docker build -f Dockerfile.rdna3 -t freetoken-rdna3:latest .
```

Then restart the server. The first start of the new image compiles its kernels again (a few minutes, once).
`rdna3/serve.sh --check` says when the image was built from another commit than the checkout. To go back:
`docker tag freetoken-rdna3:prev freetoken-rdna3:latest`, or `--image freetoken-rdna3:prev` for one run.

Each image keeps its compiled kernels in its own volume; `docker volume ls --filter name=freetoken-rdna3-kcache` lists
them, and the volume of an image you deleted can go (`docker volume rm <name>`).

- Something goes wrong: [troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md).
- Long contexts (four 262k conversations at once, or one of 1M): [long-context.md](long-context.md).
- What each profile sets and how to adapt one: [profiles.md](profiles.md).
- RAM, other GPUs, other models: [limits.md](limits.md).

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/profiles.md -->

# Profiles

A profile is one file in `rdna3/profiles/` holding every setting of one hardware setup (measured, or derived and
marked `TESTED=0`). `rdna3/serve.sh <profile>` turns it into a `docker run` + `ft serve` command (`--dry-run` prints
it); `rdna3/serve.sh --check` says which ones fit your GPUs. Speeds below are with the NVFP4 checkpoint unless a cell
names another (all three checkpoints: [README](../../README.md#which-checkpoint)).

| Profile | GPUs | Context | Decode, MTP head on (off) | Deep decode, greedy | Cold 8.3k prompt | Agent turn | At once |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `xtx-xt` | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB + RX 7900 XT 20 GB | 262,144 | 88 (65.5) tok/s | 78-96 (58-65) tok/s | 3.8 s | 0.8-0.9 s | 4 requests |
| `xtx` | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | 131,072 | 46 (41) tok/s | 36-44 (32-38) tok/s | 5.6 s | 1.5-1.6 s | 1 request |
| `xt` | RX 7900 XT 20 GB | 131,072 | 36 (34) tok/s | 29-34 (26-31) tok/s | 6.2 s | 1.6-1.8 s | 1 request |
| `xtx-xtx` *(untested)* | 2x RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | 262,144 | expected >= `xtx-xt` | – | – | – | 4 requests |
| `xt-xt` *(untested)* | 2x RX 7900 XT 20 GB | 262,144 | expected a little below `xtx-xt` | – | – | – | 4 requests |
| `gre` *(untested)* | RX 7900 GRE 16 GB | 65,536 | expected ~20 tok/s at best (head off) | – | – | – | 1 request |
| `xtx-xt-4x262k` | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB + RX 7900 XT 20 GB | 262,144 each, 4 at once | EXL3 3.05: 95.1 tok/s alone at 259k, 29.6-31.6 each with 4 | – | – | EXL3 3.05: 142-360-token turns alone 0.46-0.59 s at 224k | 4 requests |
| `xtx-xt-1m` | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB + RX 7900 XT 20 GB | 1,000,000, shared | EXL3 3.05, greedy: 84.2 / 93.0 / 84.7 tok/s at 118k / 498k / 988k | – | – | – | 4 requests |

"Decode" is one request's 512-token answers at the sampling `rdna3/serve.sh` gives (temperature 0.6; median of 12);
"deep decode" is greedy decode at every context step from 9k to 260k on two cards and 124k on one; "agent turn" is the
time to the first token when ~1k new tokens are added to a cached conversation, over the same steps (an earlier
build). The two profiles with the K/V in RAM were measured with EXL3 3.05 bpw on earlier builds
([long-context.md](long-context.md)). The profiles turn the MTP head on; `rdna3/serve.sh <profile> --no-mtp` turns it
off (numbers in brackets). All numbers:
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md). `--hybrid` (off by default) has the CPU compute part of the expert misses: NVFP4 decode +46 % on
`xtx`, +51 % on `xt`, +2 % on `xtx-xt`, measured on an earlier build than this table ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)).

## File format

```bash
GPUS=2                  # how many cards the automatic choice picks (--gpus picks them yourself)
VRAM_GIB="24 20"        # minimum VRAM per rank, used for the automatic choice
TESTED=0                # derived, not measured: serve.sh says so at start (default 1)
CTX=262144              # context length of one request (--ctx overrides); passed as --max-seq-len-override
KV_TOKENS=1050000       # the K/V pool all requests share, --kv-reserve-tokens (default: CTX, never less)
MEMORY=110g             # container RAM limit (--memory overrides)
FREETOKEN_...=...       # any other KEY=value line becomes an environment variable of the container
FT_ARGS="..."           # flags passed to `ft serve` (its --tp-size must match GPUS)
```

A comment may follow a value on the same line. Copy a file to make your own profile; it shows up in
`rdna3/serve.sh --list`.

## `xtx-xt`: two cards, tensor parallel

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `--tp-size 2` | | every layer is split over both cards, which work at the same time |
| `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT` | `0.55` | the XTX (rank 0) takes 55 % of the split work: it has more VRAM and ~14 % more compute. Measured optimum; 57.5 % and 60 % overload it during prefill |
| `FREETOKEN_TP_ALLOW_IMBALANCE` | `1` | plan memory on the smaller card (upstream refuses ranks whose free memory differs by more than 2 GiB) |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE` | `1` | dense layers in int8 (weights only, routers stay bf16): +28 % decode, frees ~2.4 GiB per card for the expert cache; lossy, agent-validated |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE` | `1` | small all-reduces through shared host memory instead of RCCL's proxies (no GPU peer-to-peer here): +2.5-4.8 % decode, bit-exact |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_TUNED` / `_DECODE_TUNED` | `1` | expert GEMM tiles swept on these cards for this model (the decode ones for this split's shapes): one prefill MoE block of 1600-2560 tokens 2.8-3.0x faster than the tiles before, long prompts -11 % on an earlier build, the down decode GEMV x1.06-1.19 in the kernel sweep, bit-exact against the default tiles |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK` | `8192` | the NVFP4 prefill MoE 8192 tokens at a time instead of 4096: cold reads +7.9 % (arms alternated, an earlier build), the same bits; 16384 left the XT 0.65 GiB of VRAM at the peak of a 255k-token read ([options.md](options.md)) |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV` | `1` | conversations evicted from the GPUs go to RAM (9.5 GiB locked) and come back in ~2 s; exact |
| `FREETOKEN_MTP` / `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M` | `1` / `4` | the checkpoint's MTP head drafts up to 3 tokens a step for a request decoding alone (up to four at once, 2 rows each past two: `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=4`, `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_DEEP=2`): +35 % decode at `rdna3/serve.sh`'s sampling (+6-13 % on one card), greedy answers unchanged; `rdna3/serve.sh --no-mtp` turns it off ([limits.md](limits.md#speculative-decoding-mtp)) |
| `FREETOKEN_SPARSE_LOGITS` / `FREETOKEN_LMHEAD_SPLIT` | `1` / `1` | a decode step's sampling needs each row's top-k only: the cards exchange their k largest logits instead of the whole vocabulary's, the draw runs in one kernel, and the LM head's rows follow the 0.55 split; the same greedy and sampled answers. One request: EXL3 3.05 bpw greedy +1.6 %, at T 0.6 +4.9 %; NVFP4 +2.6 % and +3.2 % (one run each, with the same build's flat graph positions and skipped PLE hashing; `xtx-xt-4x262k`: [options.md](options.md)) |
| `--moe-strategy offload --moe-cache-auto` | | experts live in RAM; every byte of VRAM left after the dense weights and the KV is an expert cache (7.5k of the 24,576 experts, on each card) |
| `--expert-load parallel` | | reads the expert files into RAM with parallel readers; `auto` (the engine's default) does the same but falls back to a slower serial read when free RAM is short: use `auto` on a machine with little RAM to spare |
| `--quant-backend moe.nvfp4=triton` | | the Triton NVFP4 expert kernels (the other backends need NVIDIA hardware) |
| `--ple-backend disk` | | the 51 GB n-gram embedding tables are read from the checkpoint files on demand |
| `--max-running-requests 4 --cuda-graph-max-bs 4` | | up to 4 requests decoded together (1 / 2 / 3 / 4 greedy answers sent at once finish in 3.6 / 5.9 / 8.4-8.6 / 10.1 s) |
| `--default-temperature 0.6` | | added by `rdna3/serve.sh` to every profile: requests that send no temperature get 0.6 instead of the checkpoint's 1.0 (`-- --default-temperature T` changes it) |
| `--max-prefill-length 16384` | | 16k-token prompt chunks: each chunk streams every expert once (chunks of up to 1280 tokens read only their routed experts through the cache), so bigger chunks read long prompts faster (an 8.4k prompt in 4.3 s instead of 5.5 s with 4k chunks, in the A/B that chose them) |
| `--memory-ratio 0.80` | | VRAM budget; 0.80 leaves the headroom 16k chunks need on the 20 GB card |
| `--moe-prefill-hit-d2d` | | in a chunk that streams whole layers (over 1280 tokens), experts already cached on the GPU are copied on the GPU instead of crossing PCIe again |
| `--disable-pynccl` | | ROCm uses RCCL through torch.distributed |
| `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3` | | tool calls and thinking in the model's format |
| context | 262,144 | the model's native maximum; a longer prompt is refused (`context_length_exceeded`). A 259,728-token prompt reads in 121.9 / 116.7 / 117.4 s (NVFP4 / EXL3 3.05 / 4.05 bpw) and is answered at 75.8 / 71.3 / 68.1 tok/s. The K/V of the last 12k tokens (250,000 -> 262,144) costs 134-152 expert slots per card (1.5-1.9 %) and 0.2-1.7 % of agent-turn decode, the same answers: `--ctx 250000` takes them back if you never need the full context |

With several requests, each one's decode is computed row by row as if it were alone; prompts prefilled in the same
batch can differ at rounding level. The 4-request setting, the tuned decode tiles and the RAM tier are checked for
exactness, not on the agentic benchmark ([benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#precision)).

RAM: ~83 GiB while serving, all of it locked (82 measured with an earlier build: ~63 GiB of experts, 9.5 GiB for the RAM tier, the rest the two processes; this build adds 1.2 GiB, the input embedding and the PLE row cache); ~61 GiB with the EXL3 3.05 bpw checkpoint, ~76 GiB with 4.05 bpw.

With an EXL3 checkpoint
([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)) the same profile applies: the
experts go through the EXL3 kernels (the start log says `MoE experts: exl3 via triton`), so `--quant-backend
moe.nvfp4=triton` and the `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_*_TUNED` tiles do nothing; the split rounds to whole 128-wide blocks (384 /
256, i.e. 60 / 40, which NVFP4 avoids; the EXL3 numbers are measured at it); the n-gram tables take 33 GB (3.05 bpw)
instead of 51. On two cards `serve.sh` lowers `--memory-ratio` to 0.77 (0.76 from 4 bpw): the card holding the
384-wide slice bounds the expert cache, and at 0.80 the 7900 XTX peaked 200 MiB under full VRAM
([journey.md](journey.md#16-exl3-checkpoints-2026-10-04)); `-- --memory-ratio X` overrides it.

## `xtx-xt-4x262k` and `xtx-xt-1m`: the K/V in host RAM

The `xtx-xt` settings with the attention K/V in pinned host RAM instead of VRAM, so the pool of tokens the requests
share is no longer bounded by VRAM. What differs:

| Setting | `xtx-xt-4x262k` | `xtx-xt-1m` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CTX` | 262,144 | 1,000,000 | the longest request |
| `KV_TOKENS` | 1,050,000 | unset (= `CTX`) | the pool every request shares: four full contexts (and the decode's spare page per request), or one of 1M |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_HOST` | `1` | `1` | the K/V in RAM, 14,144 bytes per token on each card (6.9 GiB per 262k conversation on two cards) |
| `FREETOKEN_ROPE_MAX_POSITION` | unset | `1048576` | positions past the 262,144 the model was trained on (the same rope below them) |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV` | `0` | `0` | no RAM tier: the pool already lives in RAM |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK` | `8192` | unset (4096) | as in `xtx-xt`; `xtx-xt-1m` keeps the default |
| `MEMORY` | `104g` | `104g` | the container's RAM limit (`110g` in `xtx-xt`) |

Measured with EXL3 3.05 bpw (~77 GiB of RAM locked by `xtx-xt-4x262k`, ~75 GiB by `xtx-xt-1m`), and NVFP4 on
`xtx-xt-4x262k` with three contexts: four do not fit with NVFP4 on 128 GB, so start it with
`rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt-4x262k --model DIR -- --kv-reserve-tokens 787500` (three conversations, 94 GiB locked after the
start), or `525000` (two) to keep room. A request alone decodes a few percent slower than on `xtx-xt` (the kernels read
the K/V across PCIe) and reads prompts a little faster (more expert slots). Which one to pick, what they cost and their
measurements: [long-context.md](long-context.md); how to count your RAM: [limits.md](limits.md#how-much-ram-do-i-need).

## `xtx` and `xt`: one card

Same settings minus the two-card ones (split, imbalance, host all-reduce, 4 requests and the verify of several at once,
the 8192-token prefill blocks). `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_DECODE_TUNED`
stays set but its table has no one-card shapes: it only logs a note. The MTP head gains less on one card (+6-13 %, +9-16 % greedy: its
verify steps mostly stay at 2 rows, the extra rows' missing experts crossing PCIe). Plus:

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `--tp-size 1` | | one card |
| `--max-running-requests 1` | | the GDN state of 4 requests would take ~2 GiB more at TP=1 (estimated) |
| `--max-prefill-length 8192` | | with 16k chunks a single card runs out of working memory: a 60k-token prompt took 166 s and decode fell to 1.9 tok/s |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV_TOKENS` / `_SNAPSHOTS` | `131072` / `16` | the RAM tier sized to the context (~5 GiB locked, estimated) |
| context | 131,072 | what fits: the XT's VRAM peaked at 19,367 of 20,464 MiB over a sweep to 124k tokens |

RAM: ~74 GiB while serving, locked (73 measured on each card with an earlier build, plus 1.2 GiB; EXL3: ~52 GiB at 3.05 bpw, ~67 GiB at 4.05 bpw).

The cards are picked by VRAM: `xt` takes the smallest card with at least 20 GiB, `xtx` the smallest with 24 GiB, so a
machine with both keeps the other card free. The one-card profiles were measured for speed, not run on the agentic
benchmark.

## The untested profiles

Derived from the measured profiles and from the memory plans the engine logged on the tested cards; `serve.sh` prints
a note when you start one (`TESTED=0` in the file).

- **`xtx-xtx`**: `xtx-xt` with an even split, the NVFP4 prefill MoE 4096 tokens at a time and drafts verified for one
  request at a time (`FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK`, `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` unset: untested on these pairs). Both cards plan on 24 GB instead of the XT's 20 GB, each holding half of
  every expert: ~9k cached experts instead of 7.5k (estimate), so decode at least as fast as `xtx-xt`. The tuned NVFP4
  decode tiles are keyed to the 0.55 split, so the even split's decode shapes use default tiles. An EXL3 checkpoint
  refuses the even split (its expert slices must be whole 128-wide blocks): add `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.6` to the file
  for it (untested, as for `xt-xt`).
- **`xt-xt`**: `xtx-xt` with an even split, 4096-token prefill blocks and drafts for one request at a time (as
  `xtx-xtx`). Each XT holds half of every expert instead of 45 %: slightly fewer cached
  experts (~6.5k, estimate), and each XT does 50 % of the split work: expect decode a little below `xtx-xt`.
- **`gre`**: `xt` on 16 GB. From the XT's plan (int8 dense weights 5.7 GiB, KV 3.1 GiB at 131k tokens, 20 % headroom)
  a 16 GB card keeps only ~3-4 GiB for the expert cache (4-7 % of the experts cached, most expert reads cross PCIe),
  with 576 GB/s of VRAM bandwidth instead of 800: ~20 tok/s at best. It starts at 65,536 tokens of context with 4k
  prefill chunks; raise `CTX` only after checking the free memory printed at start-up.

## Adapting a profile to other cards (untested)

Nothing below has been measured; treat it as a starting point and check with the benchmarks in
[testing.md](testing.md).

- **Two identical cards**: use `xtx-xtx` or `xt-xt` (`xtx-xt` without `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT`, `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK` and
  `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX`); for another identical pair
  copy one and set `VRAM_GIB`. `FREETOKEN_TP_ALLOW_IMBALANCE=1` is harmless there and needed when one card drives a
  display or runs other work (upstream refuses a free-memory difference above 2 GiB).
- **Another unequal pair**: set `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT` to about rank 0's share of the total VRAM, then try +/-2.5 %;
  `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=11:9` style weights also work (an EXL3 checkpoint moves in steps of 128 of the 640-wide
  intermediate, 20 %). The tuned NVFP4 decode tiles are keyed to this model's shapes at a 0.55 split: other splits
  fall back to the default tiles (a log line names each untuned shape once).
- **Smaller RDNA3 cards**: the RX 7900 GRE (16 GB) uses this gfx1100 image: start from `gre`. The RX 7800 XT (16 GB,
  gfx1101) needs its own image (`--build-arg GPU_ARCH=gfx1101`) and can start from `gre`; the 7700 XT (12 GB,
  gfx1101) and 7600 (8 GB, gfx1102) have less VRAM than any profile plans for. None of them is tested.
- **Less RAM**: `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV=0` saves the RAM tier (9.5 GiB on two cards, ~5 GiB on one; evicted conversations
  are re-read instead). In NVFP4 the experts themselves cannot go below ~63 GiB; the EXL3 3 bpw
  checkpoint needs 42.6 GiB: [limits.md](limits.md).

Every environment variable in these files is explained in [options.md](options.md); the `ft serve` flags in the tables
above and in upstream's [CLI reference](../cli.md).


---

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/options.md -->

# Options

Every tunable this build adds on top of upstream FreeToken is switched by an environment variable (set it in a
profile, or with `-e` on `docker run`). Unless stated otherwise the default is upstream's behavior. A few fixes have
no switch: the ROCm sampling routes, CUDA graphs for every batch size up to an explicit `--cuda-graph-max-bs` (8 or
less), the GDN boundary carried across prefill chunks, the TP>1 relay handshake, the refusal of a cache rebuild under
an uneven split, and RCCL instead of PyNCCL on ROCm ([limits.md](limits.md#does-it-work-on-nvidia-gpus)).
Measurements are from the reference machine (RX 7900 XTX + RX 7900 XT, TP=2), with the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4
checkpoint unless a row names another. Each option's effect was measured on the build that added it, as an A/B of that
option (a row says when something else changed with it): compare its two arms with each other, not with
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md). The runs behind them, with their dates: [journey.md](journey.md).

The labels:

- **Bit-exact**: the same results as without the option (identical greedy answers on a fixed set of 120 prompts, or a
  kernel check with identical outputs).
- **Reorders sums**: the same math, but floating-point additions happen in another order, so answers can differ at
  rounding level without being worse.
- **Lossy**: the numbers themselves change (8-bit weights).
- ***Agent-validated***: part of the two-card builds that scored 12-13 on the author's private agentic benchmark (29
  planted bugs, long OpenCode sessions; see [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#precision)). The one-card profiles were not
  run on it. `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT`, `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE`, `FREETOKEN_FUSE_MOE_ALLREDUCE` and `FREETOKEN_TRITON_GEMV`
  were also checked on a 671-item scored benchmark.

For every `ft serve` flag, see upstream's [CLI reference](../cli.md); the flags the profiles use are explained in
[profiles.md](profiles.md).

## Two or more GPUs

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT` | unset (even) | Uneven tensor parallelism: rank 0's share at TP=2 (`0.55`) or one weight per rank (`11:9`). XTX + XT at `0.55`: +4 % decode. With an EXL3 checkpoint the expert slices round to whole 128-wide blocks (`0.55` gives 384 / 256, the even split is refused). Reorders sums (and, with `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE=1`, changes the int8 scales of two layers: see below), *agent-validated*. |
| `FREETOKEN_LMHEAD_SPLIT` | `0`; `1` in `xtx-xt`, `xtx-xt-1m`, `xtx-xt-4x262k` | With `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT` (qwen4_exp), the LM head's vocabulary rows follow the ranks' shares instead of an even split: 136,576 / 111,744 at `0.55`. The head is bandwidth-bound (its even halves took 366 µs a pass on the XTX and 440 on the XT), and a decode step runs it ~3 times with the MTP head (up to 4). Each logit is one rank's dot product with the same K tiles: bit-exact with the int8 head (`FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE`, the profiles; `tests/layers/test_lm_head_split.py`), not checked with a bf16 head (`F.linear` may pick other kernels for other heights). With `FREETOKEN_SPARSE_LOGITS` on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (EXL3 3.05 bpw): greedy decode +0.5 %, T 0.6 +0.3 %. |
| `FREETOKEN_TP_ALLOW_IMBALANCE` | unset | `1`: accept ranks whose free memory differs by more than 2 GiB (upstream refuses them) and plan every pool on the smallest one. Needed for unequal cards; below a 2 GiB difference it changes nothing. |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE` | unset | `1` (two ranks, ROCm): small all-reduces through one shared host-memory region and a one-block kernel instead of RCCL's proxy path. 6 µs instead of ~12 µs per decode all-reduce, **+2.5-4.8 % decode, bit-exact** (fp32 accumulation, rounded to bf16 like RCCL). |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE_MAX` | `262144` | Largest message (bytes) that takes the host path; bigger ones stay on RCCL. |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE_UNCACHED` | `1` | Register the shared pages as uncached fine-grained memory (`0`: default registration). |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE_AHEAD` | `1` | The kernel loads four of the peer's 16-byte chunks a thread before it sums any (a message of up to 32 KB in one round of PCIe reads instead of one per 8 KB), each in one 16-byte load when the pages are registered uncached (two 8-byte atomic loads otherwise). The same sums, bit-identical to RCCL (`rdna3/tests/host_allreduce_check.py`). Per call in a CUDA graph, both cards: 15 KB (three decode rows) 8.4 -> 7.6-7.9 µs, 20 KB 10.0 -> 8.5, 40 KB 14.1 -> 12.0, 80 KB 23.8 -> 19.5; one row unchanged (~8 µs). In serving (`xtx-xt-4x262k`, EXL3 3.05 bpw, two runs each): +0.2 % greedy, +0.5 % at T 0.6, +0.45 % at four requests, the same answers. `0`: one chunk at a time. |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE_TIMEOUT_S` | `300` | How long a rank waits for its peer before trapping (a desynchronized pair must not hang forever); `0` = wait forever. |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_ALLREDUCE_WAITLOG` | unset | Debug, `1`: each call stores how long its rank waited for the other one (100 MHz ticks, `[rank][seq % 65536]` after the four slots), and the shared region stays in `/dev/shm` (`freetoken-hostar-*-waitlog`) for a reader inside the container until a clean shutdown (a killed container leaves it: `--ipc=host` puts it in the host's `/dev/shm`, owned by root). Same speed. On `xtx-xt` it showed the XTX waiting ~0.9 ms a decode step for the XT, at every all-reduce. |
| `FREETOKEN_TP_SYNC_TOKENS` | `1` | `1` broadcasts rank 0's sampled tokens to the other ranks after each sampled step (~15 µs per step). `0` = off; `check` also compares the ranks' draws and logs each disagreement (one sync per step). |
| `FREETOKEN_FUSE_MOE_ALLREDUCE` | `1` | qwen4_exp at TP>1: one all-reduce per MoE block (routed + shared experts) instead of two. +2.7 % decode, -4.5 % prefill time. Reorders sums, *agent-validated*. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_AR_OVERLAP` | `1` | qwen4_exp at two ranks, with `FREETOKEN_FUSE_MOE_ALLREDUCE` and the fused MoE epilogue (offloaded NVFP4 or EXL3 experts decoded on the GPU: not with `--hybrid`): a prefill chunk whose routed experts run in token blocks (`FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK`, `FREETOKEN_EXL3_PREFILL_BLOCK`) starts each block's all-reduce while the next block computes, instead of one all-reduce after the last block. Each element is the same epilogue, then the same sum of the two ranks' values: **bit-exact** (`tests/moe/test_prefill_block_hook.py`). Cold reads on `xtx-xt-4x262k` 4-6 % shorter (NVFP4 164k tokens 70.1 -> 67.0 s, EXL3 3.05 bpw 66.6 -> 62.8 s). The engine synchronizes the device once before the next decode step: without it the decode graphs ran a third slower at four requests. `0`: one all-reduce after the experts. |
| `FREETOKEN_GDN_AR_OVERLAP` | `1` | qwen4_exp at two ranks, the output projection bf16 or int8 weight-only: in a prefill chunk of one request made of whole `FREETOKEN_GDN_PREFILL_BLOCK` blocks (every 16k-token chunk of a long read but its last), each GatedDeltaNet block's gated norm and output projection run as its delta rule finishes, and that block's all-reduce starts while the next block's delta rule runs. hipBLASLt keeps the rows' bits for some shapes and block sizes only, so the first chunk of each length checks block against whole call on random data, and the ranks keep the overlap for that length only if all of them pass: **bit-exact** (`tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_gdn_ar_overlap.py`). Cold reads on `xtx-xt-4x262k`, after `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_AR_OVERLAP`, ~1-1.6 % shorter (NVFP4 164k tokens 66.9 -> 65.8 s). The check takes ~0.2 GiB for a moment, once per chunk length. `0`: the output projection after the last block. |
| `FREETOKEN_RELAY_HANDSHAKE_MAX_HELLOS` | `2400` | TP>1: how many 50 ms hellos the rank-0 relay sends while the other ranks subscribe (2 minutes). |

**`FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT`** splits the experts' intermediate dimension (routed experts on the NVFP4 Triton expert kernels,
and the shared expert) and the GatedDeltaNet heads, the last two on qwen4_exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's model code, the
only one tested); attention, the input embedding and the PLE stay even or replicated, the LM head too unless
`FREETOKEN_LMHEAD_SPLIT` ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md)). Each rank then holds a smaller or larger share of every
expert, and because the ranks all use the smallest card's expert-cache plan, the XT's smaller share raises the number
of cached experts on both cards (7,683 -> 8,708 slots when it was measured). With int8 dense layers the split also
changes the int8 scales of the two row-parallel layers it cuts unevenly (GDN output and shared-expert down
projections), not only the order of the sums.

**`FREETOKEN_TP_SYNC_TOKENS`**: every rank samples its own copy of the logits, so two different GPUs could in principle
continue on different tokens; the broadcast makes rank 1 follow rank 0. It changes no answer while the ranks agree (0
disagreements over ~8k sampled tokens in `check` mode). It is on the torch.distributed path (ROCm always; NVIDIA with
`--disable-pynccl`), and was not run on the agentic benchmark.

## Dense layers

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE` | unset | `1`: every dense (non-expert) linear layer in int8, weights only, one scale per output channel and rank; routers and the vision tower stay bf16. Converted at load. **+28 % decode**, frees ~2.4 GiB per card for the expert cache. Lossy, not bit-exact; no measurable loss on the scored benchmark, *agent-validated*. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE_SKIP` | empty | Comma-separated module names to keep in bf16. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_PREFILL_DEQUANT` | `triton` | With `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE=1`, a prefill dequantizes each int8 weight for its GEMM in one Triton pass (int8 times the row's fp32 scale, rounded once to bf16) instead of `torch.mul`'s mixed-dtype kernel: the same arithmetic, **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_int8_dequant.py`). The dequant 2-8x faster on the 7900 XT (GDN in_proj 456 -> 58 us); agent turns 0.7-1.6 % shorter on `xtx-xt-4x262k`. `torch`: `torch.mul`. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_COMPACT` | `1` | Compact the device allocator after the conversion; without it the freed VRAM stays fragmented and is lost to the expert cache. |
| `FREETOKEN_EMBED_HOST` | `1` on ROCm, `0` elsewhere | The input embedding, when it is not tied to the LM head (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's is not), stays in pinned, device-mapped host memory instead of VRAM: the same lookup kernel reads the same rows across PCIe, a 5 KiB row per token. Its VRAM (606 MiB a rank at TP=2, 1.18 GiB on one card) goes to the expert cache: on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (a 3 x 262k pool) 8,768 -> 9,255 slots with NVFP4 and 11,554 -> 12,095 with EXL3 3.05 bpw, on `xtx` 4,783 -> 5,459 (EXL3); decode 1-6 % faster, agent turns ~3 % shorter, cold reads unchanged. The same bits (`tests/layers/test_embed_host.py`). The server locks 1.2 GiB more RAM (the table). `0`: the table in VRAM. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_ROWS_MAX` | `8` | Decode batches up to this many rows (concurrent requests) use the row-looped GEMVs (the int8 one and the bf16 Triton one), each row bit-identical to a batch of one; bigger batches dequantize the int8 weight per call (bf16 layers use `F.linear`). |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_ROW_GROUPS` | `1` | With several rows (a speculative verify step, or requests decoding together), the int8 GEMVs whose input is longer than one tile (hyper-connection down projections, shared expert gate/up, index projection, LM head) read each weight tile once for up to 4 rows instead of once per row; same arithmetic per row, bit-exact. At 4 rows on the XT: HC down 17.7 -> 12.1 µs, LM head 704 -> 499 µs. `0`: each program runs the rows one after the other, reloading the tile for each. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_TP_TILES` | unset | `1` (opt-in, **not bit-exact**): K blocks of 512 for three int8 shapes of the uneven split (GDN in_proj 9270 / 7210 x 2560, attention qkv), which then run 2-4 verify rows through the row-group kernel, and an 8-wide tile for the HC up projection. Forward pass -1.5 / -2.6 / -2.9 % at 2 / 3 / 4 rows, -2.3 % at four requests on `xtx-xt-4x262k`. Each row is summed in another order, so greedy answers change at rounding level (6 of 14 prompts); not run on the agentic benchmark. |
| `FREETOKEN_HC_SILU_EPILOGUE` | `1` | Int8 decode rows: the hyper-connection's down projection stores its low-rank columns through `hc_silu` and the up projection reads them in place, instead of a kernel of its own in between (two per layer). Same bits; EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k` +1.2 % decode at one request, +1.9 % at four; NVFP4 `xtx-xt` +1.1 % and +1.1 %. `0`: the separate kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_HC_MIX_IN_GEMV` | `1` | Int8 decode rows, with the epilogue above: the hyper-connection's up projection mixes its gates into the streams as it computes them (`hc_gate_mix` inside the GEMV, its expression and stream order kept; each stream's weight row loaded once for all the rows), instead of a kernel of its own (two per layer). Same bits. At one request / four: EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k` +0.6 % / +1.4 %, NVFP4 `xtx-xt` +0.5 % / +1.1 %. `0`: the separate kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_SHARED_ACT_IN_GEMV` | `1` | Int8 decode rows: the shared expert's gate \| up projection stores SiLU(gate) x up (a program computes its gate columns and the matching up columns), instead of a SiLU-and-mul kernel after it (one per layer); only where the Triton activation is the reference (no flashinfer), and past 2 rows only for shapes whose K fits one tile (up to 4 rows for the others with `FREETOKEN_INT8_ACT_PAIR4`). Same bits. EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k` +0.8 % / +1.3 % at one / four requests, NVFP4 `xtx-xt` +0.1 % / -0.1 %. `0`: the separate kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_INT8_ACT_PAIR4` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_SHARED_ACT_IN_GEMV`: a shared expert's gate \| up projection whose K takes several tiles (NVFP4's 704 / 576 x 2560 slices, the XT's 512 x 2560 in EXL3) also stores SiLU(gate) x up at 3-4 rows (a verify step), one gate and one up column a program (`BLOCK_N` is the one tile size that keeps the sums) so that its eight accumulators fit the registers, instead of the row-group GEMV then the SiLU-and-mul kernel. **Bit-exact** (`tests/layers/test_int8_weight_only.py`). Measured with `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_ACT_IN_GEMV` below. `0`: the two kernels past 2 rows. |
| `FREETOKEN_MOE_COPY_OVERLAP` | unset | `1`: in decode, the copy of the missing experts goes to a side stream ahead of the shared expert and its gate; the expert GEMVs wait for it (offload backend, GPU decode, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). Bit-exact, but slower end to end: 47.5 tok/s decode against 71.1 without it (-33 %; one request, agent turns at 77-99k of context, MTP head on) and cold reads 13 % longer, cause not found. Leave it off. |
| `FREETOKEN_TRITON_GEMV` | `1` on gfx11 | Split-K Triton GEMVs for the bf16 decode shapes of RDNA3 (other GPUs: off). +3.5 % decode on the bf16 build; with `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE=1` only the routers are still bf16 and use it. Reorders sums (split-K), *agent-validated*. |
| `FREETOKEN_GEMV_LAST_REDUCES` | `1` | For a bf16 Triton GEMV split over K (the MoE router: 4 splits), the last of a tile's programs to finish sums the partial results (element by element, in split order, as the separate reduce kernel did) instead of a second launch; an atomic counter per tile, reset by that program. **Bit-exact**, 48 launches fewer per decode step; measured together with `FREETOKEN_FEWER_COPIES` below. `0`: the reduce kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_GEMV_SHARED_TILES` | `1` | For a bf16 Triton GEMV split over K (the MoE router) at 2-4 rows (a verify step): each weight tile is loaded once for all the rows instead of once per row, each row summed over the same tile in the same K order. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_gemv_shared_tiles.py`: every row equal to the row alone). In a CUDA graph, the router (512 x 2560) at four rows 11.2 -> 7.4 µs on the 7900 XTX, 14.0 -> 9.3 on the XT; one row unchanged. `0`: a tile load per row. |

## Experts (MoE)

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_MOE_MISS_READS` | `1` | Decode on the expert cache (offload backend, EXL3 and NVFP4 Triton kernels): the expert GEMVs read a slot the cache is filling this step straight from the layer's pinned host bank (across PCIe) and write it into the slot on the way, instead of the cache copying it before the GEMVs start: the transfer overlaps the GEMV work of the experts already cached. The cache still copies the small banks first (EXL3's rotation scales, NVFP4's global scales). The same words, the same sums: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_exl3_miss_reads.py`, `tests/kernels/test_nvfp4_miss_reads.py`: the outputs and the filled slots are those of copying first). `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs each, with `FREETOKEN_BANK_COARSE`: EXL3 3.05 bpw one request +0.9 % greedy, +1.6 % at T 0.6, four requests +4 to +10 %; NVFP4 +2.1 %, +2.6 %, four requests +3 to +7 %; the same answers. `0`: the cache copies every bank first. |
| `FREETOKEN_ROUTER_SHARED` | `1` | Decode on the expert cache, a MoE layer of up to four rows: the router's bf16 GEMV and the shared expert's int8 gate \| up GEMV with its activation in one launch, then the shared expert's down projection and the router's softmax top-k in one launch (each pair reads one input, or nothing of each other): the programs of both kernels, their bodies unchanged, at the warps the shared expert's tiles run at (the router GEMV's sums do not depend on them). Two launches fewer a layer. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_router_shared.py`, at every row count and the shared expert's widths of both checkpoints and splits). `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs: EXL3 3.05 bpw one request +2.5 % greedy, +2.3 % at T 0.6, two and four requests +0.2 / +0.4 %; NVFP4 +2.4 %, +2.3 %, +0.1 / +0.3 %; the same answers. `0`: four launches. |
| `FREETOKEN_MOE_ENSURE_COPY` | `1` | Decode on the expert cache with `FREETOKEN_MOE_MISS_READS`: a layer's slot admission (flashlib's LRU `lru_ensure`, the same code) and the copy of the small banks of the experts it admits run in one launch instead of two; the other programs of the launch wait for the admission's plan, then copy. The same slots, plan and bytes: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_moe_ensure_copy.py` compares the cache state, the plan and the copied rows with the two kernels' over 60 steps). EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs: one request +0.7 % greedy, +0.5 % at T 0.6, four requests within the noise; the same answers (NVFP4: the same answers, measured with the other changes of its build). `0`: the two launches. |
| `FREETOKEN_BANK_COARSE` | `1` on ROCm | The pinned host banks of the experts are registered coarse-grained (`hipExtHostRegisterCoarseGrained`): the GPU's L2 may keep lines it reads from them (the banks never change once filled). A GEMV reading a missing expert from its bank (`FREETOKEN_MOE_MISS_READS`) then moves it at the copy kernel's speed: an EXL3 gate \| up slice (0.74 MB) in 32.5 µs against 58.8 fine-grained, where the copy kernel takes 33.6 either way (7900 XTX). Cold reads: NVFP4 0.8 % longer (96k-214k tokens, `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs), EXL3 unchanged. `0`: fine-grained, as `cudaHostRegister` registers them. |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_TUNED` | unset | `1`: NVFP4 expert GEMM tiles for prefill swept on RX 7900 XTX / XT for this model, chosen by token count (any split, one or two cards). Only the M / N tiles, warps and stages change (a different K tile would reorder the sums): **bit-exact**, the bits of upstream's default tiles (16 to 8192 tokens, checked on one card). One prefill MoE block of 1600-2560 tokens 2.8-3.0x faster than the tiles it replaced, 1280 tokens 1.4-1.5x; prefills of up to 1536 tokens (agent turns, a few rows an expert) take 4-warp tiles (NVFP4 one-word turns at 26k 0.350 -> 0.227 s on `xtx-xt-4x262k`, an earlier build); long prompts -11 % on the prefill GEMM before upstream's rewrite. |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_DECODE_TUNED` | unset | `1`: the same for decode (upstream's marlin decode kernel), per (N, K) and batch size, for the two-card shapes at a 0.55 split; other shapes (one card, other splits) keep the default tiles, logged once per shape. The down GEMV x1.06-1.19 in the kernel sweep (gate_up keeps the default tiles, the best of the sweep). **Bit-exact** against the default tiles. |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_ACT_IN_GEMV` | `1` | NVFP4 decode (the marlin GEMV): the routed experts' gate \| up GEMV stores SiLU(gate) x up itself, a program computing its gate columns and the matching up columns with the GEMV's own K loop and tiles, rounded as the GEMV stores them, then the Triton activation kernel's expression; one launch fewer per MoE layer. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_nvfp4_act_in_gemv.py`). Not where flashinfer is installed (its activation is another reference). With `FREETOKEN_INT8_ACT_PAIR4`, on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (NVFP4, against both off, two pairs): one request 100.6 -> 101.3 tok/s greedy (+0.8 %), 103.7 -> 104.5 at T 0.6 (+0.9 %); four requests within the noise; the same answers. `0`: the GEMV then the activation kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_BLOCK` | `4096`; `8192` in the `xtx-xt` and `xtx-xt-4x262k` profiles | The prefill MoE runs the chunk this many tokens at a time on the same expert banks (`0` = the whole chunk). The block size changes no bit (`rdna3/tests/moe_block_check.py`, both cards; greedy answers and an agent conversation identical at 8192 and 16384). Its temporaries grow with it, ~75 KiB a token on the 7900 XTX's slice (~600 MiB at 8192), and the cache planner does not set them aside. 8192 instead of 4096: cold reads +7.9 % (arms alternated, an earlier build); 16384 read faster again but left the XT 0.65 GiB of VRAM at the peak of a 255k-token read, hence 8192. One card keeps 4096 (8k chunks, less working memory). |
| `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_TAIL_TILES` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_NVFP4_PREFILL_TUNED=1`, a prefill block of more than 6144 tokens: each expert's rows past its last full 128-row tile run in 32-row tiles of a second launch, in both GEMMs, instead of a 128-row tile mostly padding (an expert gets ~160 rows of an 8192-token block on average). Only the M / N tiles, warps and stages change: **bit-exact** (`tests/moe/test_prefill_tail_tiles.py`). One 8192-token MoE block 16-19 % faster with random routing, 11-12 % with this model's own; cold reads of 113-210k tokens ~5-6 % shorter on `xtx-xt-4x262k`, between two earlier builds that also differed by `FREETOKEN_ROW_STORE_RINGS` (which alone moves such reads by 1 % at most). `0`: one launch of 128-row tiles (64 for the down GEMM). |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_MID_COLS` | `32` | EXL3: in prefill (more than 256 routes, fp16), the step between the two expert products rotates 32 columns of the Hadamard at a time, 32 rows and 4 warps a program, instead of 64-row tiles. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_exl3_mid_cols.py`); 1.7-3.3x faster, with 572 B of scratch per lane instead of the tile kernel's 2.7 KB (a dispatch of it waiting for that scratch once held a rank before an all-reduce until the 60 s watchdog: [journey.md](journey.md#27-agent-turns-short-prefills-through-the-expert-cache-2026-10-14)). `0`: the tile kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_ROTATE_BLOCKS` | `5` | EXL3 decode: from 40 rotated vectors up (a verify step's rows x the routes x gate and up), a program of the input rotation takes this many 128-blocks instead of one: ~1,600 tiny programs at four rows. The same `_had128_vec` on the same tile per block: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_exl3_rotate_blocks.py`). In a CUDA graph on the 7900 XTX: four rows 14.7 -> 9.4 µs, eight 28.3 -> 18.7 (the XT 37.9 -> 20.3); one row keeps one block a program (6.7 against 8.5 µs grouped). `1`: one block a program. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_VEC_WARPS` | `2` | EXL3 decode: warps of an input-rotation or mid-step program (`1`, `2` or `4`). Each program's 128 x 128 product and reduction (`_had128_vec`) keeps its order at 1, 2 and 4 warps (not at 8): **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_exl3_rotate_blocks.py`). At 2 instead of 4, in a CUDA graph: the mid step at four rows 8.7 -> 5.1 µs on the 7900 XTX, 10.7 -> 5.6 on the XT, at eight rows 12.4 -> 6.2 and 14.6 -> 7.0; the rotation at four rows (five blocks a program) 9.8 -> 7.2 and 11.9 -> 8.3. The output step (`tl.dot` tiles) keeps 4 warps: others are slower or change its bits. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_SHARED_ROUTES` | `4` | EXL3 decode at two rows or more (a verify step, several requests): the routes that read the same expert share a GEMV program, up to this many (`1`, `2` or `4`), which decodes each trellis tile once for all of them; each route keeps its own sums in the single-route order. Which program takes which routes is written by the input rotation's kernel (no launch of its own). **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_exl3_shared_routes.py`: every route, the whole decode MoE layer). A third of the routes share an expert at four rows of one request, a third at four requests of two rows (recorded routing). The whole decode MoE layer in a CUDA graph on that routing, the 7900 XTX's 384-wide slice: four rows 131 -> 111 µs, four requests 227 -> 195, two rows 79 -> 78; the XT's 256: 117 -> 101, 199 -> 168, 79 -> 75. In serving (`xtx-xt-4x262k`, EXL3 3.05 bpw, two pairs): one request +1.8 % greedy, +2.3 % at T 0.6, four requests +1.8 to +5 %, the same answers. NVFP4's GEMVs gain nothing from it (their decode is cheap). `1`: one program a route. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_PREFILL_BLOCK` | `4096` | EXL3 checkpoints ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)): the prefill MoE runs 4096 tokens at a time (`0` = the whole chunk); its temporaries (540-620 MiB on the 384-wide expert slice) are kept free by the cache planner at start. The block size changes no result (`rdna3/tests/exl3_moe_check.py`), except that a block of 25 tokens or fewer (the last one included) takes decode kernels for some of its steps and rounds differently. 8192 read 2-2.5 % faster but left 504 fewer expert slots (of 11,117), hence 4096. Blocks of up to 512 tokens (agent turns) run 16-row tiles instead of 32 (always on, the same bits): the MoE block 11-19 % faster at 32-512 tokens. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_PREFILL_TAIL_TILES` | `1` | EXL3 checkpoints, a prefill block of 3072 tokens or more: the gate-up GEMM runs each expert's full 64-row tiles in one launch and its remaining rows in 32-row tiles in a second one (the down GEMM keeps its 32-row tiles: no gain there). The same K order: **bit-exact** (`tests/moe/test_prefill_tail_tiles.py`). Cold reads of 113-210k tokens 1.4-1.6 % shorter on `xtx-xt-4x262k`. `0`: one launch of 32-row tiles. |
| `FREETOKEN_ROUTER_KEYS` | `1` on ROCm | The MoE router's top-k (a softmax over the experts, one wave a row) picks each expert with one reduction of 64-bit keys (the value's ordered bits, then the inverted expert id: the largest value, the lowest id among equal ones) instead of three (the largest value, the lowest id holding it, the winner's weight by a masked sum), and computes the winner's weight with the softmax's own operations on that value. The same experts, order and weight bits (`tests/kernels/test_router_keys.py`: bf16 and fp32 rows full of equal values, signed zeros, infinities, NaN, fewer finite values than picks). In serving the kernel takes 5-7 µs a call against 10-15 with `0` (traced; ~50 calls a step with the MTP head). `xtx-xt-4x262k`, EXL3 3.05 bpw, two runs each (an earlier build of this path, without the check for rows of fewer finite values than picks): one request greedy 94.5 -> 95.6 tok/s (+1.2 %), four requests +1.0 %; at T 0.6 101.4 -> 102.7 (+1.3 %, one run each); the same greedy and sampled answers as with `0`. `0`: the three reductions. |
| `FREETOKEN_HYBRID_FETCH_FRACTION` | unset | With `--moe-strategy hybrid` ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)): the share of each decode step's expert misses fetched over PCIe (strictly between 0 and 1), the rest computed on the CPU, the same share on every MoE layer (`rdna3/serve.sh --hybrid` sets `0.25` on one card and `0.4` on two with NVFP4, `0.6` with EXL3). Unset: the split `ft bench bw --model <checkpoint>` measured for each layer's kind, or a fixed cap of one fetch per layer without one (EXL3 is not benched). |
| `FREETOKEN_HYBRID_MIN_REQS` | `1` | With `--moe-strategy hybrid`: decode steps of fewer requests fetch every miss (the offload path). CUDA graphs are captured per batch size, so each size takes one path. `rdna3/serve.sh --hybrid` does not set it. |
| `FREETOKEN_HYBRID_FLAG_IN_KERNEL` | `1` | With `--moe-strategy hybrid`: one kernel writes the CPU's inputs into its pinned IO rows and rings the coordinator, another waits for the CPU's partial and adds it back, over two pinned flag words (`0`: upstream's copies around the doorbell's stream memops, ~3.2 us a node). Bit-identical. With the other hybrid kernels, one request on NVFP4 `xtx-xt` 74.3 -> 78.3 tok/s, measured with an earlier handshake that these replaced, not again since ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)). Replaces `FREETOKEN_HYBRID_SPLIT_KERNEL`. |
| `FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_GROUP` | `1` | CPU expert executor, NVFP4 / bf16: one task per (expert, row block) for the routes of rows that share an expert, so its rows are read from RAM once (`0`: one task per route). Bit-identical. |
| `FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_ROUTE_STATS` | unset | Measurement: every `n` CPU expert tasks, print how many of the CPU's routes repeat an expert of another row of the same step (8-13 % in the `--hybrid` runs). |
| `FREETOKEN_HYBRID_SKIP_CPU_ROUTES` | `1` | With `--moe-strategy hybrid`, NVFP4 and EXL3: the GPU decode kernels write zeros for the routes the CPU computes (slot -1) instead of computing them on slot 0 at weight 0. Bit-identical; +1-3 % decode ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)). |
| `FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_CORES_BY_SLICE` | `0` | `1`: under tensor parallelism each rank's CPU expert pool takes a share of the cores proportional to its expert slice (an uneven `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT`) instead of half. Measured without gain. |
| `FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_SMT` | `0` | `1`: the CPU expert pool also runs on its cores' SMT siblings. 5-11 % faster alone on the CPU (EXL3), 14-42 % slower in serving. |
| `FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_EXL3_COLS` | `1` | EXL3 on the CPU: adjacent tile columns per task, the first prefetching their contiguous row segments. 7-8 % less CPU time on 31 threads alone, within the noise in serving. |
| `FREETOKEN_BATCH_MEMCPY_ROCM` | unset | Copy engine for `--moe-prefill-hit-d2d` on ROCm: `batch` = `hipMemcpyBatchAsync` (HIP >= 7.1), `loop` = one copy per entry (full-layer short prefills ~10 % slower); unset tries `batch`, then `loop`, and logs a mode that fails its probe. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_HIT_LOG` | unset | `1`: log, per prefill chunk, the share of expert rows reused from the GPU cache instead of crossing PCIe. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_CACHED_MAX` | `1280` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, `0` otherwise | A prefill chunk of at most this many tokens (an agent's tool result) reads its routed experts through the slot cache: only the ones it lacks cross PCIe, those the next layer is predicted to need copied while this one computes (`FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT`), instead of streaming every expert the cache lacks through the full-layer buffers; `0` = off. Decided once per forward, so every layer takes the same path; off when a layer is a CPU or unpinned one, or when the expert cache is several slot pools or holds fewer slots than two layers of experts. The same bits; the experts it brings in are the next to be evicted, so the decode after the turn keeps its cache. EXL3 3.05 `xtx-xt-4x262k`, 25k of context, measured with a top-14 prediction (`FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT_EXTRA=4`; the default top-10 is faster still: see `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT`): 132-339-token turns 0.76-0.79 -> 0.50-0.56 s to their first token, ~1k-token turns 0.84-0.88 -> 0.76-0.82 s, unchanged above the threshold ([journey.md](journey.md#27-agent-turns-short-prefills-through-the-expert-cache-2026-10-14)). Under `--hybrid` the answers then move, as any change of the cache's contents moves them there ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)). |

## Qwen3.8-Flash-Next specifics

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_SYNC` | `auto` | How a captured decode step gets its PLE disk rows. `auto` probes the stream memops once at start: `wait-sync` (the step waits inside the graph for the host fill) where a captured wait holds three replays in a row (ROCm 10 on these cards); else `launch-gating` (the host fills before each launch). On one GPU without the MTP head (the scheduler then overlaps its decode steps) `auto` takes `launch-gating`: wait-sync costs ~11 ms a step there (NVFP4 `xtx --no-mtp`: 26.6 tok/s against 38.3). The log says which. `wait`: require memops, `gate`: never use them. Elsewhere wait-sync gives +1.6-4.3 % decode over launch-gating, bit-exact. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_PREFILL_PREFETCH` | `1` | With `--ple-backend disk` (every profile): a thread reads a prefill's PLE rows from the checkpoint while the layers before the PLE layer launch (the lookup waits for them), and while a chunk of a longer prompt computes it reads the next chunk's rows into the other pinned buffer, instead of a read before each forward with the GPUs idle (~1.1 s for a 16k-token chunk on the reference NVMe). The same rows: **bit-exact** (`tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple_disk.py`). `xtx-xt-4x262k`: cold reads of 96-164k tokens ~14 % shorter (EXL3 3.05 bpw 164k 62.1 -> 53.4 s), agent turns 2-3 %; decode unchanged. `0`: the read before each forward. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_DRAFT_READS` | `1` | With `--ple-backend disk`, decoding with the MTP head: the next step's PLE rows are read on a thread while the GPU drafts, into a 16,384-row RAM cache of the decode store (the first token's once the verify step's kept tokens reach the host, each draft's once the head has drawn it; the thread polls for them with short sleeps, HIP's event wait spinning a core for the whole wait, except for the last draft, whose read the fill waits for); the step's own fill then finds them there instead of reading every row from disk after the drafts. The bytes of the reads: **bit-exact** (`tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple_disk.py`). On `xtx-xt-4x262k` (EXL3 3.05 bpw, one request) the fill after the drafts 0.75 -> 0.17 ms, 99 % of its rows found in the cache; decode +0.7 % greedy, +0.5 % at T 0.6 (two pairs); four requests unchanged (the fill 1.1 -> 0.2 ms there too, but the host reaches each step after the GPU has finished the one before: its readback wait is ~0). `0`: the fill reads them all. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_PREFILL_RANK0` | `1` | With `--ple-backend disk` at TP>1: only rank 0 reads a prefill's PLE rows from disk and broadcasts their bytes to the other ranks at the lookup (every rank stages every head, so the bytes are the same: **bit-exact**), instead of every rank reading the same rows at once from the same disk. Agent turns 4-7 % shorter on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (EXL3 3.05 bpw 0.466 -> 0.435 s, NVFP4 0.693 -> 0.662 s); decode and four requests unchanged. `0`: each rank reads its own. |
| `FREETOKEN_ROW_STORE_RINGS` | `4` | The disk row store (`--ple-backend disk`, every profile): a fill of 256 rows or more splits over this many io_uring rings, one thread each. One thread drove 240-290k reads a second whatever its queue depth; the reference machine's NVMe (PCIe 3 x4) takes ~490k a second from four. A row that crosses a 4 KiB page is read as its two pages, apart: on that disk, reads spanning two 4 KiB units, even 2.5 % of a batch, halved the whole batch's rate. The same bytes: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_row_store.py`). 9,600 random rows (a 600-token turn's) 40-42 -> 21-26 ms; on `xtx-xt-4x262k` EXL3 3.05 bpw agent turns 0.525 -> 0.494 s, NVFP4's (PCIe-bound) ~1-2 % with the tail tiles. `1`: one ring. |
