| `FREETOKEN_PLE_ROW_CACHE_ROWS` | `1048576` | With `--ple-backend disk`: a RAM cache of the PLE rows read before (8-way, least recently used out) in the store that reads the prefills (rank 0's at TP>1; decode steps keep reading the disk): an agent session's n-grams recur across its turns (simulated over this repository's source files read one a turn, ~40 % of a turn's rows had been read by an earlier turn). 176 MiB of RAM with NVFP4's rows, 118 MiB with EXL3's. The bytes the disk gives: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_row_store.py`). `xtx-xt-4x262k`: ~2,600-token turns on a 45k conversation 4-5 % shorter (NVFP4 1.21 -> 1.16 s, EXL3 3.05 bpw 0.99 -> 0.94 s), ~520-token EXL3 turns ~1 %, NVFP4's unchanged (PCIe-bound); cold reads unchanged. `0`: no cache. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_PLAN_KERNEL` | `1` | The QSA layers' per-forward index-write plan (compressed-slab rows, ring rows, the mrope rows of the indexer) in two kernels instead of ~30 torch ops, in the graph and in each eager MTP pass (four times a 4-row step). Same values. With `FREETOKEN_PLE_CONV_KERNEL` and `FREETOKEN_MTP_KV_ONLY_STOP`: EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k` +1.8 % at one request, +1.9 % at four; NVFP4 `xtx-xt` +1.6 % / +1.0 % ([journey.md](journey.md#25-a-decode-step-kernel-by-kernel-2026-10-11-and-12)). `0`: torch ops. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_FUSED_WRITES` | `1` | In each QSA layer, after the group compression, the index keys' norm and rope into the compressed slab, the indexer queries' norm and rope and the raw keys' store into the pending ring run as one launch (`qsa_index_writes`) instead of three: each part is its kernel's code on its own tile, on disjoint memory. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_qsa_fused_writes.py`); two launches fewer per QSA layer (~28 a decode step). Measured with `FREETOKEN_QSA_FUSED_GATE` below. `0`: three launches. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_FUSED_GATE` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_FEWER_COPIES`: the attention's output gate (`o * sigmoid(gate)`) is applied by the QSA backend in the split-K merge of the sparse attention when there is one (decode), with `_sigmoid_gate_mul_kernel`'s operations on the merge's bf16 output; one launch fewer per QSA layer. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_qsa_fused_gate.py`). With `FREETOKEN_QSA_FUSED_WRITES`, on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (EXL3 3.05 bpw, against both off, one pair and the image twice): one request greedy 99.6 -> 100.0-100.5 tok/s, at T 0.6 105.1 -> 105.5-106.0; four requests within the noise; the same answers. `0`: the gate's own kernel. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_CONV_KERNEL` | `1` | The PLE's decode conv over a verify step's rows in one kernel instead of ~6 torch ops a row, on gfx11 (other GPUs keep the torch ops). Same bits (fp32 products rounded on their own, summed in the order torch takes there). `0`: torch ops. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_CONV_BLOCK` | `4096` | The per-layer-embedding (PLE) convolution runs 4096 tokens at a time, for one or several requests. Keeps big prefill chunks and batched prefills within memory (3 requests prefilled together, 16k tokens: 0.7 GiB of temporaries, 2.6 GiB unblocked). Reorders sums; *agent-validated* for one request, identical to the unblocked path in a GPU check with several. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_CACHED_MAX`: layer L+1's router applied to layer L's MoE input predicts the experts layer L+1 routes to (each token's top-k: 79-84 % of them, and about as many it does not route to), and the ones not cached are copied on a copy stream while layer L computes; layer L+1 copies only what the prediction missed. Only copies, so the same bits. `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT_EXTRA` (default 0) adds candidates per token: +4 caught 88-91 % but copied more experts that were not routed to, and short turns ran up to 6 % slower on EXL3 `xtx-xt-4x262k`. `0`: no prediction (and the cache path off by default: without the prediction it gained only below ~300 tokens and lost from ~1k on). |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT_MIN_VOTES` | `auto` | With `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT`: copy ahead only the experts at least this many of the chunk's tokens predict; the others, when layer L+1 routes to them, go through the fix-up copy. Only copies: **bit-exact** (`tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_predict_votes.py`). An NVFP4 agent turn of 500-750 tokens copied ~10,000 predicted and ~1,600 missed experts on rank 0 (~16 GiB, PCIe saturated), many of the predicted ones named by a single token and not routed. `auto`: 2 with NVFP4 experts (`xtx-xt-4x262k`: agent turns 0.663 -> 0.625 s, one-word turns 0.245 -> 0.229 s), 1 (every prediction) otherwise: EXL3 turns ran 1-7 % slower at 2, as they lean on the copies overlapping the compute. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREFETCH_DEFER` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREDICT`: the predicted experts' copy plan, which the copy engine needs on the host, is copied to pinned memory with an event and read once the layer's expert GEMMs are queued, instead of right after the plan: a sync at every layer (~47 a short turn) that emptied the GPU's queue, which then refilled at the host's launch pace. The same copies into the same slots: **bit-exact** (`tests/moe/test_prefill_cached.py` runs both ways). `xtx-xt-4x262k`: EXL3 one-word turns 0.246 -> 0.220 s, agent turns 0.508 -> 0.494 s; NVFP4 one-word turns 0.263 -> 0.258 s, agent turns unchanged. `0`: the read right after the plan. |
| `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_COPY_OVERLAP` | `auto` | With `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_CACHED_MAX`: the routed experts a short prefill's prediction missed are copied on the prefill copy stream while the shared expert runs, instead of before it on the compute stream. The same copies and GEMMs: **bit-exact**. `auto`: with the experts decoded on the GPU (not with `--hybrid`, not measured there), EXL3 ones only with `FREETOKEN_PREFILL_PREFETCH_DEFER` (with the plan read right after it, the EXL3 decode after the turns ran 1-2 % slower: [journey.md](journey.md#33-short-turns-the-host-waiting-at-every-layer-2026-10-18-and-19)). `xtx-xt-4x262k`: short turns 2-6 % shorter (NVFP4 agent turns 0.407 -> 0.399 s, EXL3 0.488 -> 0.476 s), decode unchanged. `1` / `0`: on / off whatever the experts. |
| `FREETOKEN_FUSED_MOE_EPILOGUE` | `1` | The routed experts' sum, the shared expert's gate (a dot product and a sigmoid) and the mul-add of each MoE block in one kernel instead of three; the NVFP4 decode hands over its per-expert outputs. Same arithmetic in the same order on the same tiles: **bit-exact**. Only Triton NVFP4 / EXL3 experts on the GPU decode path, at TP=1 or with `FREETOKEN_FUSE_MOE_ALLREDUCE=1` (hybrid and CPU layers add partial sums); others keep the three kernels. NVFP4 `xtx-xt` greedy decode 57.8 -> 59.2 tok/s without the MTP head, 82.9 -> 83.8 with it. `0`: three kernels. |
| `FREETOKEN_FUSED_HC_NORM` | `1` | Each hyper-connection combine and the grouped RMSNorm that reads the streams next (the MLP block's, the next layer's, the final mixer's; not into a PLE layer) in one kernel, the normed streams freed as soon as read. **Bit-exact**, two launches fewer per layer. With the epilogue above, `xtx-xt` greedy decode with the MTP head: NVFP4 82.9 -> 85.6 tok/s, EXL3 3.05 bpw 86.4 -> 89.2, 4.05 bpw 81.6 -> 83.3; prompt reading and VRAM peaks unchanged ([journey.md](journey.md#19-fewer-decode-kernels-2026-10-06)). `0`: separate kernels. |
| `FREETOKEN_FEWER_COPIES` | `1` on ROCm, `0` elsewhere | Decode and prefill read the attention's q / k, its output gate, the GDN gate z and the QSA indexer's q / k where the projections wrote them, instead of copying each to a contiguous tensor first: the norms and the indexer kernels take the strides, the gate is applied in one kernel (the sigmoid rounded to bf16 as torch does), and the K/V store reads v from the qkv projection's rows (k and v each with its own row stride). **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_fewer_copies.py`, `tests/kernels/test_jit_index_store.py`); up to ~110 launches fewer per verify step. With `FREETOKEN_GEMV_LAST_REDUCES`, `xtx-xt` greedy with the MTP head, an earlier build without the v store: NVFP4 83.2 -> 85.1 tok/s, EXL3 3.05 bpw 99.1 -> 101.9; prompt reading unchanged; VRAM peak ~100 MiB lower. The v store (one copy fewer per attention layer, ~14 a decode step) with `FREETOKEN_PLE_DRAFT_READS`, against the build before both (`xtx-xt-4x262k`, EXL3 3.05 bpw, two pairs): one request +1.7 % greedy, +1.4 % at T 0.6, four requests +0.9 %; the draft reads alone +0.7 / +0.5 / 0 %. Off on NVIDIA: flashinfer's `gemma_rmsnorm` takes 2D inputs only, and the bits were checked on ROCm's Triton only. `0`: the copies. |
| `FREETOKEN_QK_NORM_ROPE` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_FEWER_COPIES`, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's attention layers: the per-head q and k RMSNorms and the 3-axis rope in one launch instead of three: one program per row and head runs the norm as the Triton norm kernel does (the same code, tile and warps, so the same sum), stores it, then rotates the head's first `rotary_dim` dims as the rope kernel does. **Bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_qk_norm_rope.py`); prefill row counts where the two norms would run at different warps keep the three launches. NVFP4 `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs: one request +0.5 % greedy, +0.5 % at T 0.6, two and four requests +0.4 / +0.3 %; the same answers. `0`: the three launches. |
| `FREETOKEN_EXL3_RECON_FP64` | `1` | EXL3 checkpoints: the two Hadamard products that rebuild the dense weights at load run in fp64 instead of fp32, so the bf16 weights do not depend on the GEMM kernel the BLAS picks: in fp32, ROCm 10.0 and 10.1 rebuild other weights, hence other EXL3 answers (10.1's hipBLASLt changed its batched kernel); in fp64 the same weights. Differs from the fp32 rebuild in 0.02-0.03 % of the weights (one unit in the last place). Load time unchanged. `0`: fp32. |
| `FREETOKEN_HC_INPLACE` | `1` | Each hyper-connection combine writes the new streams over the old ones, and the PLE output is added to the streams in place (a long one-request prefill adds it block by block, without the PLE's own output tensor). The same sums, the same bits; each [T, 5 x hidden] tensor avoided is 320 MiB at a 16k-token chunk. `0`: new tensors, as upstream. |
| `FREETOKEN_GDN_CONV_ROWS` | `1` | The GatedDeltaNet prefill conv (Triton path) reads the projection's q / k / v columns in place and writes each group token-major into its own buffer (`causal_conv1d_varlen_rows`), instead of a channel-major transpose of its input and strided copies of every 4096-token block's q / k / v. The same kernel and taps: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_conv_rows.py`). Cold reads of 98k and 116k tokens +3.5 to +4.2 % tok/s (NVFP4 `xtx-xt-4x262k`, arms alternated). A forward whose token count times the projection width passes 2^31 (~175k tokens; the chunks are 16k) takes the channel-major conv, whose offsets are 64-bit. `0`: the channel-major conv. |
| `FREETOKEN_GDN_PREFILL_BLOCK` | `4096` | The GatedDeltaNet delta rule of a prefill runs 4096 tokens of each request at a time, the recurrent state carried through the request's pool slot (a multiple of 64; `0`: the whole chunk in one call). The same bits (the kernels work per 64-token chunk with an fp32 state); a quarter of the temporaries at a 16k-token chunk. |
| `FREETOKEN_GDN_PREFILL_WARPS` | `8` on ROCm | Warps of two GatedDeltaNet prefill kernels (the state recurrence of `chunk_delta_h`, upstream 4; `recompute_w_u`, upstream 4 warps and 3 stages, here 1 stage). At upstream's they spill 484 and 796 B per lane to scratch on RDNA3. The same bits; a 16k-token GDN prefill 37 % faster on a 7900 XT (8.56 -> 5.43 ms), and less of the scratch the HIP runtime takes outside the torch allocator (101 -> 48 MiB). `0`: upstream's launches. `SGLANG_GDN_CHUNK_H_NUM_WARPS` still overrides the first. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_MIN_WARPS` | `4` on ROCm | The fewest warps of the QSA sparse attention kernel. Its prefill profile (tuned on GB300) runs 2 warps, which on RDNA3 at head_dim 256 spill ~2.2 KB per lane to scratch; at 4 none. The same bits (bf16 cache; 8 prefill shapes of 128-16k rows checked); the kernel 39-45 % faster at 1k-16k rows, and no ~60 MiB of scratch per GPU queue outside the torch allocator. Decode already runs 4. `0`: the profile's own. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_SCORE_ROWS` | `1` | The QSA indexer's block scoring of a prefill of one request (64 rows or more) runs 16 query rows a program instead of one: each tile of compressed keys is loaded once for the 16 rows and their 4 heads together. The same K order and head sums as the one-row kernel: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_qsa_score_rows.py`, both cards). A 16k-token chunk 150k deep: 47.3 -> 11.1 ms a layer on the 7900 XTX; cold reads of 96k and 164k tokens 3-6 % shorter on `xtx-xt-4x262k`. `0`: one row a program. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_INT8` | unset | **Not recommended.** `1`: int8 KV cache for the attention (QSA) layers, 3.19 -> 1.71 GiB per card. Short benchmarks and 227k-token needle tests looked fine, but the agentic benchmark fell from 12-14 to 8-9 bugs fixed and the agent stopped exploring early. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_STAGE_SELECTED` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_HOST=1`, a prefill copies to VRAM only the K/V rows of the tokens it selects (marked per layer by the attention kernel's own mapping) instead of every page in use: the attention reads the same rows, so the same bits (`tests/kernels/test_qsa_kv_host.py`). A 220-row turn at 224k selects 11-21 % of the history's tokens. EXL3 3.05 `xtx-xt-4x262k` at 224k of context: turns of 142-360 tokens 0.57-0.70 -> 0.49-0.62 s, 1.0-1.1k 0.90-0.98 -> 0.84-0.89 s, the same answers; unchanged at 25k. `0`: every page in use. |
| `FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_HOST` | unset | `1` in `xtx-xt-1m` and `xtx-xt-4x262k`. `1`: the attention K/V slab in pinned, device-mapped host memory instead of VRAM, so the pool the requests share is bounded by RAM, not VRAM ([long-context.md](long-context.md)). Decode and verify read the selected tokens across PCIe; a prefill first copies the rows its tokens select to VRAM (`FREETOKEN_QSA_STAGE_SELECTED`). Bit-identical answers. On ROCm the memory is allocated non-coherent, so L2 keeps what the verify rows share. Decode a few percent slower than with the K/V in VRAM (EXL3 3.05 bpw at 118k: 86.6 tok/s with a 262k page table, 84.2 with a 1M one, 90.6 in VRAM), more expert slots. The pool stays at `--kv-reserve-tokens` (a page past it would pin ~0.9 MB of RAM for ~0.1 MB of VRAM); `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV=1` is ignored with it (a warning) and `FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_INT8=1` refused. |
| `FREETOKEN_ROPE_MAX_POSITION` | unset | `1048576` in `xtx-xt-1m`. `N`: the plain rope's table runs to N positions instead of `max_position_embeddings` (262,144), so one request can go past the positions the model was trained on. Below 262,144 the table is the same, so shorter contexts get the same bits. With `1048576` the model kept its retrieval and its next-token loss flat to 988k tokens ([long-context.md](long-context.md#quality-past-262144-tokens)). |

## Speculative decoding with the MTP head (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next)

The checkpoint ships a multi-token-prediction head (`mtp.*`: one decoder layer with its own 512 experts). With it, a
decode step of one request verifies the head's guesses in the same forward: m rows (the last token, then m - 1
drafts), of which it keeps the matching prefix. How it works and what it costs:
[decisions.md](decisions.md#speculative-decoding-with-the-mtp-head), measurements:
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#speculative-decoding-mtp-head). The profiles except `gre` turn it on (`FREETOKEN_MTP=1`,
`FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M=4`); `rdna3/serve.sh --no-mtp` serves without it.

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_MTP` | unset (`1` in the profiles) | `1`: load the MTP head and draft with it; its experts share the expert cache (an NVFP4 checkpoint's stacked bf16 head experts are quantized to NVFP4 at load, an EXL3 checkpoint's are read as they are). Only with `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M` > 1 (else a warning, and no head) and a checkpoint whose head experts are in one of those two forms (others are refused). |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M` | `1` (`4` in the profiles) | The most rows a verify step runs (1 + drafts). With the head, `4` is the measured setting (the adaptive depth then picks 2-4 rows per request); greedy answers stay identical to plain decode with `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE=1`, as every profile sets (bf16 dense layers outside the GEMV table go through `F.linear`, whose sums can change with the row count) and the default fp32 GDN state (`FREETOKEN_MAMBA_SSM_DTYPE`). Without the head, `m` > 1 runs placeholder rows (a cost measurement only). |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_MS` | `1,2,..,M` with the head | The row counts a step may run, each with its CUDA graphs (counts above the smallest only for the batch sizes a verify step can have). Near a request's length limit a step runs no more rows than tokens left. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_DYNAMIC` | `1` | Each request picks its rows per step (2 to M, at most 2 past `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_DEEP` requests; with `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` > 1, the most any of the step's requests wants) from its running acceptance per draft position and the step costs below: the count with the most expected tokens per millisecond (with two or more row counts above 1, as by default). `0`: always M. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_COSTS` | measured, by card count | Step time per row count (ms; only the ratios matter): two cards (`xtx-xt`) `1:17.7,2:25.3,3:30.7,4:35.5`, one card (`xt`) `1:31,2:53,3:78,4:102`, where the extra rows' missing experts cross PCIe and the adaptive depth mostly keeps to 2 rows. Entries given here override. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` | `1`; `4` in `xtx-xt`, `xtx-xt-1m`, `xtx-xt-4x262k` | Verify drafts only while at most this many requests decode (at most `--cuda-graph-max-bs`, checked at start). With more, steps run one row per request, the head only writes its KV (so drafts stay good when a request is alone again) and scheduling overlaps as without the head. `2` against `1` (`xtx-xt`, an earlier build): two agents at ~100k of context decode 33.6-34.4 tok/s each instead of 30.8-31.1, 2-3 short requests finish 3-4 % sooner, 1 and 4 requests take the same time; a sweep to 248k ran without an out-of-memory retry. More than 2 rows each at four requests lose (an earlier build: four requests at 4 rows each 26.3 tok/s against 35.35 without verifying), hence `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_DEEP=2` beside it. Greedy answers as with `1`; past 8 rows per step answers can change. `xtx-xtx` and `xt-xt` leave it unset (not measured there). |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_DEEP` | `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX`; `2` in `xtx-xt`, `xtx-xt-1m`, `xtx-xt-4x262k` | More than 2 rows per request only while at most this many requests decode (at most `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX`); past it, up to `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` requests, a step verifies 2 rows each and the head drafts one guess (1 row and no drafts if `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_MS` has no 2). Each row of a wide step brings its own missing experts, so the second row pays where the third and fourth do not: four requests (NVFP4, `xtx-xt-4x262k`, one row count for every step) 31.3 tok/s each at 1 row, 35.2 at 2, 31.7 at 3, 30.4 at 4. `4` / `2` against `2` / `2` on `xtx-xt-4x262k`: three requests +6-9 % each, four +3-6 % greedy (-0.3 to +2.5 % at T 0.6), one request unchanged; `xtx-xt` and `xtx-xt-1m` gain at three requests too ([benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#several-requests-and-agents-at-once-xtx-xt)). At the profile's own 1,050,000-token pool (EXL3 3.05 bpw, one run each): three requests 43.1 -> 45.9 tok/s each, four at T 0.6 38.2 -> 39.3; cold reads, decodes at 28k-130k of context and agent turns unchanged, 17 of 17 answers the same. Greedy answers the same on prompts read apart; four sent at once can differ, as between two runs without it (their prompts are read in one batch). At most 8 rows per step; a step of 3-4 requests no longer overlaps with the next one's scheduling, as a verify step must not. Two more CUDA graphs per card: ~280-380 MiB less VRAM free after the capture, the expert slots unchanged. |
| `FREETOKEN_MTP_KV_ONLY_STOP` | `1` | While more than `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` requests decode, the head's pass only writes its KV: it stops once the K/V and the index keys are written instead of attending and combining (nothing reads that output). The same KV. `0`: the whole pass. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_GLUE_KERNELS` | `1` | A verify step's glue in kernels: the rollback copies (one kernel per state instead of ~6 ops), the token-pool writes, the kept counts of greedy rows, the head's rows and each chained guess's addressing; the acceptance log summed on the host. Same values. One request +1.5 % on EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k` (greedy answers on fixed texts), +1.6 % on NVFP4 `xtx-xt`. `0`: torch ops. |
| `FREETOKEN_STEP_INPUTS` | `1` | A decode step replayed from a CUDA graph (QSA attention): the scheduler writes the step's inputs (each row's position and mrope positions, each request's page-table row, GatedDeltaNet slot, K/V length, and the token-pool write tuple) into one pinned buffer; one copy to the GPU and one kernel then write the graph's input buffers (the token and the K/V slot each row reads, the QSA block table) instead of ~25 small copies, casts and gathers a step. The same values in the same buffers: **bit-exact** (`tests/kernels/test_step_inputs.py` for the kernel; answers identical in serving). EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k`, two pairs: one request +0.8 % greedy, +0.7 % at T 0.6, two requests +0.7 %, four +1.2 %. `0`: the copies. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_ROLLBACK_SKIP` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_SPEC_GLUE_KERNELS`, a request that kept every row of its verify step copies no GatedDeltaNet state back (it is already in place) instead of writing that copy to the padding slot, as the torch path's fixed-shape `index_copy` does (only that slot, which no live request owns, sees a difference). Each copy moves the request's states of every layer (~35 µs a call at one request, ~130 at four, several calls a step). `xtx-xt-4x262k`, EXL3 3.05 bpw, two runs each: +0.5 % greedy and at T 0.6, +0.6 % at four requests greedy, +0.1 % at T 0.6; the same answers. `0`: the copy to the padding slot. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPARSE_LOGITS` | `0`; `1` in `xtx-xt`, `xtx-xt-1m`, `xtx-xt-4x262k` | ROCm, TP > 1, with the MTP head: a decode step's LM head keeps each rank's shard of the logits. A step whose choices need only each row's largest logits (greedy rows, or sampling from a `top_k` of at most 256, no penalties) all-gathers every rank's k largest (two Triton kernels a shard) instead of the whole vocabulary's logits, and a kernel merges them into the values, ids and order `torch.topk` of the whole row gives (one row: equal values by ascending index; several rows: its bitonic sort's order) and `torch.argmax`'s pick. Other steps gather the whole rows as before; the engine runs one such gather at start (the first all-gather of a process sets up RCCL's path for it, 0.9 s, which the first request's prefill paid otherwise). Bit-exact: the same greedy and sampled answers (the sampled texts identical to the whole-row path's in every run), except for a logit of exactly -0.0, +0.0 or NaN among a row's k largest (`torch.topk` orders those otherwise than `torch.argmax`, and one merge follows the latter). With `FREETOKEN_SAMPLE_KERNELS` and `FREETOKEN_LMHEAD_SPLIT` on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (and two smaller changes of the same build: the graphs' positions in one flat buffer, no GPU hashing for the disk PLE store), two runs each: EXL3 3.05 bpw one request greedy 94.1 -> 95.1 tok/s (+1.0 %), at T 0.6 95.2 -> 99.8 (+4.8 %), four requests +1.1 % / +2.5 %; NVFP4 (a 300k-token pool) 94.8 -> 96.5 (+1.8 %), at T 0.6 94.0 -> 99.3 (+5.6 %), four requests +2.1 % / +6.4 %. |
| `FREETOKEN_SAMPLE_KERNELS` | `1` | With `FREETOKEN_SPARSE_LOGITS`, a verify step's speculative sampling and a draft's draw from rows of at most 64 candidates run in one Triton kernel each (`kernel/triton/spec_sampling.py`) instead of ~60 and ~25 torch ops, with their bits: torch's `exp` and `log` on gfx1100 (LLVM's AMDGPU expansions, written out), its softmax, sum and cumsum orders (the last two change with the row width and count: reproduced for the shapes served), the same `torch.rand` calls. Checked bit for bit against the torch ops (`tests/kernels/test_spec_sampling.py`) and in serving (the same sampled texts). At T 0.6, one request: +2.0 % against the torch ops on the same texts. Each new kernel variant compiles the first time it runs: the engine compiles those of the checkpoint's default `top_k` at start, 14.5 s at the first start of an image (Triton's cache keeps them: 0.5 s after). `0`: the torch ops. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_SAMPLED_DRAFTS` | `1` | A sampled request's drafts are draws from the head under the request's own temperature / top-k / top-p, verified against that distribution, instead of the head's argmax (both exact speculative sampling; greedy requests keep the argmax, so greedy answers do not change). A drawn draft is kept with probability Σ min(p, q), the argmax with p(argmax): more tokens kept per step. At `serve.sh`'s T 0.6 on `xtx-xt-4x262k`: 14 prompts x 1024 tokens NVFP4 91.0-91.5 -> 94.0-94.2 tok/s, EXL3 3.05 bpw 92.9-93.0 -> 97.0; long contexts (28k-130k) NVFP4 the same, EXL3 +7 %; two requests at once within 1.5 %. Each arm samples other texts (the draws fall differently), so single prompts move -9 to +18 %. At T 1.0 the same speed (an earlier build). `0`: the argmax. |

## Sampling

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_FAST_TOPK_MAX` | `256` on ROCm, `0` elsewhere | When every request of the batch has a `top_k` of at most this value (the model's default is 20), the batch samples from its top-k candidates only: one `torch.topk` + one small kernel, ~0.07 ms per step, exact. Otherwise the batch takes the full-vocabulary path (below). |
| `FREETOKEN_SAMPLE_ARGS_REUSE` | `1` | A decode step whose requests sample under the same parameters as the step before reuses that step's device tensors of them (temperatures, top-k, top-p, greedy mask; read-only downstream) instead of copying them to the GPU again: four host-to-device copies fewer a sampled step. The same values: **bit-exact**. `0`: copied every step. |

On ROCm, top-k / top-p sampling never uses upstream's cooperative kernels: their multi-block rows spin on a barrier
that needs every block of a row running at once, which the cooperative launch does not give on this ROCm stack (they
hang on gfx1100), and with one block per row their top-p costs 10-60 ms per step. The full-vocabulary path takes an
exact threshold from a sort instead: 0.2 ms (1 request) to 1 ms (4 requests), the same kept set as the float64
definition, and for a given seed the same draws as upstream's kernels except when a draw lands within fp32 rounding of
a boundary between two tokens. One request without `top_k`, or with a larger one, sends its whole batch there. At a
tie on the k-th logit the top-k path keeps exactly k tokens, the sorted path keeps all the tied ones. The sorted path
is checked by kernel tests, not run on the agentic benchmark (greedy decoding and the model's default `top_k` of 20 do
not use it).

## Conversations kept in RAM

For hybrid models (attention + GatedDeltaNet, e.g. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). When the GPU context memory is full, the least
recently used conversation parts are copied to pinned RAM instead of being dropped, and copied back when their
conversation returns. Exact: a conversation brought back gives the same greedy answer as one that never left (four
conversations checked). Checked for exactness, not on the agentic benchmark.

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV` | unset | `1`: enable. For several conversations that together outgrow the GPU pool, such as parallel sub-agents: a returning conversation is copied back instead of read again from scratch ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#conversations-kept-in-ram)): four agents with 82-117k-token conversations, 3 turns each, got their first token in ~2 s instead of ~47 s after the first reads. No gain for a single conversation that fits the GPUs; costs the pinned RAM below. |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV_TOKENS` | `262144` | RAM tier size in tokens (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, TP=2: 4.91 + 4.59 GiB pinned for the two ranks with the MTP head, 4.64 + 4.32 without, with the snapshots below). |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV_SNAPSHOTS` | `24` | GatedDeltaNet state snapshots kept in RAM (50-65 MB each at TP=2). |
| `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV_LOG` | unset | `1`: log every move to and from RAM. |

Beyond the GPU pool + the RAM tier, the least recently used conversations are dropped as upstream does.

## Scheduling

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE` | `0` | `N`: after each prefill chunk, the requests already decoding get up to N decode steps before the next chunk. Keeps other agents moving during a long read, but measured to hurt the short prefills of agent turns: alone, keep `0`; see `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE_LONG`. |
| `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE_LONG` | `0` | `1`, with `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE=N`: the N decode steps follow only a chunk that leaves prompt to read (a long read), never a turn read in one chunk, so agent turns are as without it. Prefill first otherwise (upstream's policy): a request decoding while another reads a long prompt waits for the whole read. EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt-4x262k`, one request decoding while a 130k-token prompt is read cold (one run each): the read 38.1 s and the decoding request stopped for 38.0 s without it; `N=8` 39.1 s (+2.7 %) and stops of at most one chunk (4.9 s), 124 stream chunks reaching it during the read against 35; `N=32` 42.2 s (+10.8 %), 402. The decoding request's own answer is unchanged in length and speed once the read is over. |
| `FREETOKEN_VRAM_MARGIN_MIB` | `512` on ROCm, `0` elsewhere | Once the engine is built, cap the torch allocator at the card's VRAM minus what lives outside torch then (HIP runtime, RCCL, loaded kernel modules, scratch, a desktop's buffers: the card's used VRAM is read from sysfs, since the free memory HIP reports leaves the graphics stack out) minus this margin. A prefill that reaches the cap makes the allocator release its cached blocks, or fail with a plain out-of-memory error, before the card is full: within tens of MiB of full the driver's evictions ended in GPU page faults and a hung collective ([troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md#a-gpu-fault-or-a-hung-collective-with-a-full-card)). The cap and the VRAM outside torch are logged at start. `0`: no cap. |
| `FREETOKEN_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE` | `8` | The tokenizer keeps the last N prompts it encoded. A prompt that shares a prefix with one of them takes that prompt's tokens up to the last turn start (`<\|im_start\|>`) inside the shared part and encodes only the rest: the same tokens (a fast tokenizer encodes the text between two added tokens on its own; the split is checked on probe strings at start, else off; `tests/tokenizer/test_prefix_cache.py`). An agent turn's encode at 173k of context ~0.4 s -> 2 ms: a short turn's first token 0.93-1.03 -> 0.53-0.58 s (EXL3 `xtx-xt-4x262k`), the same answers. `0` = off. |
| `FREETOKEN_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CHECK` | `0` | `1`: also encode every prompt whole, log a mismatch and keep the whole encoding (validation). |
| `FREETOKEN_TRITON_FAST_LAUNCH` | `1` | A Triton launch skips Triton's per-launch Python (the binder specializing every argument, the cache key, the launch metadata and two empty launch hooks): the kernel compiled for a launch is kept under a key computed from what that specialization reads (each tensor's dtype, 16-byte alignment and storage under 2 GiB; each integer's 1 / multiple of 16 / width; the constexprs and options), and later launches with the same key call its launcher directly. The same compiled kernel with the same arguments: **bit-exact** by construction (`tests/kernels/test_triton_fast_launch.py`). A launch took ~18 us of host time in isolation (~10 us this way) and ~50 us in the server, and a short agent turn launches ~1,550: EXL3 one-word turns 0.235 -> 0.214 s on `xtx-xt-4x262k`, NVFP4 (PCIe-bound) 0.260 -> 0.255 s. A launch hook (a profiler), a pre-run hook, an argument type the key does not cover, or a Triton other than 3.8.0 takes Triton's path (no `Triton launches: fast path` line in the log then). `check`: also runs Triton's binder at every launch and raises if it would pick another kernel (validation). `0`: Triton's path. |
| `FREETOKEN_MLOCK` | `1` | Lock the process's memory once the model is loaded (`mlockall`, current and future pages, on fault), so that with `vm.compact_unevictable_allowed=0` the kernel's memory compaction leaves the pages the GPU driver maps alone; each move stopped the GPU queues for seconds ([troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md#long-pauses-in-the-middle-of-a-run)). Skipped, with a log line, under a finite `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`. `0`: off. |

## Diagnostics (off by default)

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `FT_STATS_EVERY=N` | Every N graph-replayed decode steps, log the host step period vs the GPU time of the forward. |
| `FT_MOE_STATS=1` | With `FT_STATS_EVERY`: also the expert-cache miss counters. |
| `FT_PROF_STEPS=N`, `FT_PROF_START=S` | torch.profiler over N decode steps from step S; tables and a chrome trace in `FT_PROF_DIR`. |
| `FREETOKEN_DUMP_PROMPT_TOPK=<dir>` | Tests only: rank 0 saves the top-40 log-probabilities and the input ids of every prefill chunk to `<dir>/prompt-<n>.pt` (teacher-forced comparisons; send raw completions, a chat user turn mostly measures `<\|im_end\|>`). Needs `FREETOKEN_MTP=0`; at 1M of context, `--max-prefill-length 4096`. |
| `FT_PROF_EAGER=1` | Also profile eager decode (run with `--cuda-graph-max-bs 0`): ROCm's profiler does not see kernels replayed from a CUDA graph. |
| `FT_PROF_STACK=1` | With `FT_PROF_STEPS`: also record Python stacks and input shapes; the chrome trace then ties each kernel to the line that launched it (ops by input shape in `rank<r>_ops_by_shape.txt`). |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_TIMING=N` | Every N decode steps, the GPU and host time of each phase (forward, verify, MTP head, draft chain) per (requests, rows); one stream sync per report. |
| `FREETOKEN_SPEC_STALL_MS` | `500`; with `FREETOKEN_SPEC_TIMING`, every decode step whose GPU or host time, or distance to the previous step, exceeds it is logged on its own with its phases and the time of day (every rank): to catch the occasional stall. |
| `FREETOKEN_PLE_FILL_TIMING=N` | Every N decode steps, the host's wait for the step's tokens and the PLE disk fill time after it (the GPU idles through the fill when stream memops are unavailable). |

`FT_PROF_DIR` defaults to `./ftprof`, i.e. `/opt/FreeToken/ftprof` inside the container, which is lost when the
container stops: set `FT_PROF_DIR=/root/.cache/freetoken-rdna3/ftprof` to keep it in the kernel-cache volume, or
`docker cp` it out first.

## PyTorch TunableOp

Not used: tuning the dense GEMMs of the 16k-token prefill chunks gained 1.5-1.7 % on those GEMMs and < 0.2 % on
prompt reading ([journey.md](journey.md#17-dropped-along-the-way)). Never enable tuning in service
(`PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_TUNING=1`): each new prompt length would be tuned on the spot (16 s prefills).

## Container settings the engine does not check

`PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` and `OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE` (set by `serve.sh`; the engine also turns
expandable segments on by itself when neither `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF` nor `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF` is set; without expandable
segments the allocator's cache filled the free VRAM and every 14-16k-token prefill chunk past ~26k of context failed
once and retried after emptying it, with or without the MTP head and with a larger margin too), an explicit
`HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (rank 0 first), `--ulimit memlock=-1` (pinned RAM for the experts and the RAM tier) and
`--ipc=host` (shared memory between the two ranks). `TVM_FFI_CACHE_DIR` (set by the image and `serve.sh`) keeps the JIT
modules in the per-image cache volume: without it they are rebuilt at every start (first request ~10 s instead of
1.3-1.9 s).


---

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/benchmarks.md -->

# Benchmarks

Everything here was measured on one machine: RX 7900 XTX 24 GB + RX 7900 XT 20 GB (gfx1100, PCIe 4.0 x16 each, no GPU
peer-to-peer), Threadripper 3970X, 128 GB DDR4-3200, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4 (RadixArk checkpoint; the
EXL3 checkpoints in [their depth sweep](#depth-sweep-exl3-checkpoints) and
[how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)).

The summary and the three depth sweeps are the numbers re-measured at each release
([maintaining.md](maintaining.md#releasing)). The sections after them come from earlier builds than the summary and
give orders of magnitude; a section that mixes the two says so.

## How the numbers are taken

- **Servers**: one server per row, started by `rdna3/serve.sh`, each profile as shipped (MTP head on) and NVFP4 again
  with `--no-mtp`, with the host settings of
  [troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md#long-pauses-in-the-middle-of-a-run). The first server of each checkpoint and
  card count runs a second time once the image's kernel cache is warm, and that run is the one shown: in the first, the
  kernels compile during the depth sweep's first pass (NVFP4 `xtx-xt` read its 16k step at 1416 tok/s, 2079 in the
  second pass).
- **Decode, one request**: tokens/s of 512-token answers after the first token, thinking off: the median of 12 answers
  (6 prompts x 2: English and French prose, code, a recipe) at the sampling of a request that sets none (the
  checkpoint's top-k / top-p, temperature 0.6 from `rdna3/serve.sh`), and 3 greedy answers.
- **Cold prefill (PP)**: an 8.3k-token prompt with nothing cached, time to first token (`rdna3/bench/quick_bench.py`).
- **Depth sweep** (`rdna3/bench/depth_sweep.py`): one conversation grown in steps up to the profile's maximum context.
  The first step is a cold ~8.8k-token read; each later step adds a 6-52k-token block the cache has not seen, like a
  large tool result (ten steps to 260k on two cards, seven to 124k on one). At each step: **TG** = greedy decode over
  256 tokens, **PP** = speed of reading that block, **agent turn** = time to the first token of a following ~1k-token
  turn (an earlier build for this column: since the short-prefill changes, 200-250-token turns take 11-13 % less time to
  their first token on another workload, [journey.md](journey.md#31-short-agent-turns-2026-10-17-and-18)). Median of two
  passes, each with its own text. With the MTP head, TG follows how many of its guesses the text lets it keep (1.6-3.5
  tokens per step): the spread between steps is the text, not noise.

## Summary

| Profile | Decode, one request: sampled / greedy | TG, 9k to max depth | Cold 8.3k prompt (PP) | PP of a new block | Agent turn, 9k -> max | Max depth |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `xtx-xt` | 88.2 / 86-90 tok/s | 78-96 tok/s | 3.8 s, ~2220 tok/s | 1910-2180 tok/s | 0.9 -> 0.9 s | 260k |
| `xtx-xt --no-mtp` | 65.5 / 66-69 tok/s | 58-65 tok/s | 3.8 s, ~2200 tok/s | 1980-2170 tok/s | 0.9 -> 0.9 s | 260k |
| `xtx` | 45.9 / 42-48 tok/s | 36-44 tok/s | 5.6 s, ~1500 tok/s | 1520-1670 tok/s | 1.5 -> 1.5 s | 124k |
| `xtx --no-mtp` | 40.6 / 37-43 tok/s | 32-38 tok/s | 5.5 s, ~1520 tok/s | 1560-1680 tok/s | 1.5 -> 1.6 s | 124k |
| `xt` | 35.8 / 33-38 tok/s | 29-34 tok/s | 6.2 s, ~1340 tok/s | 1350-1480 tok/s | 1.7 -> 1.7 s | 124k |
| `xt --no-mtp` | 33.6 / 30-35 tok/s | 26-31 tok/s | 6.0 s, ~1380 tok/s | 1410-1510 tok/s | 1.6 -> 1.7 s | 124k |
| `xtx-xt`, EXL3 3.05 bpw | 94.4 / 86-95 tok/s | 95-117 tok/s | 3.6 s, ~2340 tok/s | 1940-2280 tok/s | 0.7 -> 0.9 s | 260k |
| `xtx-xt`, EXL3 4.05 bpw | 80.5 / 79-84 tok/s | 86-94 tok/s | 3.6 s, ~2330 tok/s | 1970-2270 tok/s | 0.8 -> 1.0 s | 260k |
| `xtx`, EXL3 3.05 bpw | 55.8 / 56-61 tok/s | 52-58 tok/s | 5.0 s, ~1680 tok/s | 1700-1820 tok/s | 1.0 -> 1.2 s | 124k |
| `xtx`, EXL3 4.05 bpw | 45.3 / 44-48 tok/s | 37-47 tok/s | 5.1 s, ~1630 tok/s | 1640-1820 tok/s | 1.3 -> 1.4 s | 124k |
| `xt`, EXL3 3.05 bpw | 43.2 / 42-45 tok/s | 41-46 tok/s | 5.5 s, ~1500 tok/s | 1500-1600 tok/s | 1.2 -> 1.3 s | 124k |
| `xt`, EXL3 4.05 bpw | 34.9 / 34-36 tok/s | 29-36 tok/s | 5.7 s, ~1450 tok/s | 1450-1620 tok/s | 1.5 -> 1.5 s | 124k |

The EXL3 rows ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)) were measured the same way, one server per row
started by `rdna3/serve.sh` (on two cards it lowers `--memory-ratio` to 0.77 / 0.76 for EXL3), MTP head on, the same
scripts: the 12 sampled and 3 greedy answers, `quick_bench.py` for the
cold read, the depth sweep. The checkpoints answer differently, so the MTP head keeps a different share of its
guesses: read the decode columns across checkpoints as an order of magnitude.

With the head, one request decodes 35 % faster on two cards at the sampling above (+35 to +60 % greedy along the
sweep) and 6-13 % faster on one card (+9 to +16 % greedy); reading a block takes from 5 % longer (`xt`) to 1 % less. With more
requests decoding than `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX` (4 in `xtx-xt` and its K/V-in-RAM variants, 1 in the other profiles),
the head only writes its KV: see the tables further down.

Without the head, decode loses 11 % from 9k to 260k on two cards and 16 % from 9k to 124k on one card (with it,
the text of each step decides how many drafts are kept). Where the one-card drop
comes from (`xtx`, one pass with `FT_STATS_EVERY=64 FT_MOE_STATS=1`, on an earlier build): the decode step takes ~27 ms
of GPU time at 9-16k and ~33 ms from 25k to 124k, flat beyond 25k, while the expert cache misses ~2.2 then 3.0-3.6 of
the 10 experts a layer reads: the longer context spreads the routing over more experts (the misses do not fall during
an answer, so it is not the prefill evicting the cache), and attention itself adds little.

|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8.8k | 88.2 / 64.8 | 2191 / 2172 | 0.88 / 0.89 s |
| 16.0k | 91.6 / 64.7 | 2108 / 2093 | 0.90 / 0.90 s |
| 25.0k | 96.3 / 61.8 | 2163 / 2146 | 0.93 / 0.93 s |
| 40.0k | 88.6 / 58.2 | 2184 / 2169 | 0.80 / 0.94 s |
| 60.0k | 94.1 / 59.0 | 2105 / 2160 | 0.87 / 0.89 s |
| 86.9k | 83.8 / 59.3 | 2121 / 2170 | 0.85 / 0.87 s |
| 122.9k | 92.7 / 59.2 | 2058 / 2125 | 0.86 / 0.86 s |
| 164.9k | 80.1 / 58.2 | 2034 / 2093 | 0.87 / 0.87 s |

| 259.8k | 86.7 / 57.7 | 1909 / 1975 | 0.90 / 0.89 s |

Each sweep ran after the decode answers and `quick_bench.py` on the same server. The ~1k-token agent turn takes
0.8-0.9 s at every depth: such a turn reads only its routed experts through the expert cache and reuses the previous
prompt's tokens ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#short-chunks-agent-turns)).

Each cell: TG (tok/s) / PP of the new block (tok/s) / agent turn. On two cards the agent turns take 0.70-0.94 s at
3.05 bpw against 0.80-0.93 s with NVFP4: such a turn copies the routed experts the cache lacks
([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#short-chunks-agent-turns)), and a 3.05 bpw expert weighs 1.86 MB against 2.76 MB (not measured
apart).

## Agent turns on real code (`xtx-xt`)

Conversations built from this repository's own source and docs (77-113k tokens), then 8 turns each: a ~2k-token tool
result and a ~250-token answer, temperature 0.6 (what the reference machine's agent client sends). An earlier build,
when `xtx-xt` verified drafts for at most two requests (`FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=2`; now 4):

| Per request | With the head | Without |
|---|---:|---:|
| One conversation: decode | 71.1 tok/s | 55.8 tok/s |
| One conversation: time to the first token of a turn | 1.75 s | 1.73 s |
| Two conversations at once (sub-agents), `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=1`: decode | 31.1 tok/s | 33.2 tok/s |
| Same, `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=2`: decode | 33.6-34.4 tok/s | |
| Two conversations at once: time to the first token | 1.96 s | 1.95 s |

Two requests share each decode step. With `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=1` the head then only writes its KV, so each gets
~31-33 tok/s at ~100k of context, with or without it; with `2` it keeps verifying drafts for both. On the reference
machine's own launcher settings (image input on): 36.4 against 31.6 tok/s each, and with thinking on 38.8
against 34.2 on the turns the two decode together; two conversations of 115k and 121k tokens decoded together with no
out-of-memory retry.

## Several requests and agents at once (`xtx-xt`)

| Workload | Result |
|---|---|
| Decode, 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 requests at once, greedy 512-token answers, counted while every request decodes (median of two passes) | with the head 72.3 / 81.9 / 82.2 / 89.2 tok/s in total (72.3 / 40.9 / 27.4 / 22.3 per request); without it 59.5 / 79.2 / 85.6 / 92.3 (59.5 / 39.6 / 28.6 / 23.1) |
| 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 requests at once, greedy answers of 93-200 tokens, time from the send to the last token (two rounds) | with the head 3.6 / 5.9 / 8.4-8.6 / 10.1 s; without it 4.1-4.2 / 5.9-6.0 / 8.2-8.3 / 9.8 s |
| 5 requests with different sampling settings (greedy, T=1, top-p only, top-k 1000 + top-p decoding together; top-k 20 + top-p queued behind them), 256-token answers | ~27-28 tok/s for each of the 4 decoding together |

In `xtx-xt` and its K/V-in-RAM variants three and four requests verify too, 2 rows each (`FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=4`,
`FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_DEEP=2`), against the setting before (`2` / `2`: 3-4 requests run one row each). On `xtx-xt-4x262k`, greedy 768-token
answers unless noted, tok/s per request, two runs each, a 300k-token pool, the MTP head drafting under each request's
sampling:

| Requests | NVFP4 before -> now | EXL3 3.05 bpw before -> now |
|---|---:|---:|
| 3 at once | 38.4 -> 40.8-40.9 | 44.4 -> 48.3 |
| 4 started 1.5 s apart | 34.2-34.3 -> 35.3-35.4 | 41.0-41.9 -> 43.6-43.7 |
| 4 at once (512 tokens) | 31.3-32.8 -> 33.8-33.9 | 38.3 -> 40.2-40.3 |
| 4 started apart, T 0.6 | 32.4-33.3 -> 32.0-33.5 | 40.5-41.2 -> 41.8-42.0 |
| 1 (four 768-token answers in turn) | 95.9-96.0 -> 95.8-96.0 | 97.0 -> 96.9-97.1 |

With 2 to 4 rows each at four requests (NVFP4, every step at that count): 35.2 tok/s at 2 rows, 31.7 at 3, 30.4 at 4,
31.3 with one row.

With `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=1` (an earlier setting of `xtx-xt`; the untested `xtx-xtx` and `xt-xt` keep it), only a
request decoding alone verifies drafts: with two or more, steps run one row per request and the head only writes its KV,
an eager pass that cost 3-4 % at 3-4 requests on `xtx-xt` (an earlier build); a lone request finishes 13 % sooner.

A request's decode is computed the same way alone or batched (per-row kernels); prompts prefilled in the same batch can
differ at rounding level, as they already do with prefix caching.

## Speculative decoding (MTP head)

`FREETOKEN_MTP=1 FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M=4` (adaptive depth), each profile without the head against the same plus the
head (one server per configuration; the odd half of the 120-item set). Greedy answers identical with and without the
head on every profile (5 chat prompts, the 60 items, the 108k-token turns, the functional checks). The
[summary](#summary) and the depth sweeps give one request's decode with and without the head; by kind of work:

| One request, decode tok/s (or time) | `xtx-xt` | `xtx` (2 rows) | `xt` (2 rows) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 chat prompts x 2, median | 57.7 -> 74.8 | 38.0 -> 40.3 | 31.2 -> 32.7 |
| 3 agent turns on a 3.5k-token prompt | 51.5 / 58.9 / 54.3 -> 71.8 / 65.4 / 66.5 | 34.9 / 38.5 / 32.4 -> 37.6 / 40.3 / 34.7 | 28.8 / 30.7 / 27.4 -> 29.8 / 31.7 / 28.5 |
| 108k-token prompt, then a follow-up turn | 56.4 / 55.4 -> 71.0 / 76.2 | 35.1 / 35.1 -> 38.0 / 39.0 | 29.1 / 28.8 -> 31.5 / 31.7 |
| Time to the first token of that prompt | 56.8 -> 59.2 s | 78.7 -> 82.4 s | 84.5 -> 88.4 s |
| One 1500-token answer | 59.8 -> 73.9 | - | - |
| 60 code / math items (time) | 296 -> 215 s | 516 -> 473 s | 613 -> 563 s |

On `xtx-xt` a request keeps 1.9-3.9 tokens per step (512-step averages). The one-card columns ran at 2 rows, their
answers identical to plain decode (-: not measured at 2 rows), except their times to the first token, which come from
the run with the two-card step costs below.

On one card the extra rows cost more: its expert cache holds ~2.3k (XT) or ~3.5k (XTX) of the 24.6k experts against
~7k per card on `xtx-xt`, and a 4-row step on the XT misses 8-10 experts per layer against 2-3 in plain decode (all
copied over PCIe): 93-98 ms against ~31. With the two-card step costs (mostly 4 rows) the head made one card slower
(chat prompts: `xtx` 38.0 -> 34.6 tok/s, `xt` 31.2 -> 27.6; the other figures of that run in
[journey.md](journey.md#15-speculative-decoding-with-the-mtp-head-2026-10-01)). At 2 rows (53 ms) the head pays; the
one-card step costs make the adaptive depth keep to 2 rows (`xt`: chat 32.6 / 29.8 / 36.3 tok/s against 30.9 / 28.9 /
32.2 without the head).

Step costs (`xtx-xt`, NVFP4, `FREETOKEN_SPEC_TIMING=64` over decode, concurrency and prompt-reading runs, contexts up
to ~41k tokens; GPU ms per step, phases summed):

| Requests x rows | 1 x 2 | 1 x 3 | 1 x 4 | 2 x 2 | 2 x 3 | 2 x 4 | 3 x 1 | 4 x 1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Step (forward + verify + head + draft chain) | 25.3 | 28.8 | 36.4 | 39.7 | 53.1 | 65.0 | 36.3 | 44.5 |
| Of which the forward | 21.4 | 25.2 | 31.7 | 35.5 | 48.6 | 59.1 | 35.6 | 43.9 |
| Steps measured | 1640 | 1745 | 1434 | 25 | 68 | 272 | 1022 | 1022 |

These runs used `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=2`: with three or four requests a step ran one row each and the head only wrote
its KV (now 2 rows each in `xtx-xt` and its K/V-in-RAM variants, [above](#several-requests-and-agents-at-once-xtx-xt)).

## Precision

- **Scored benchmark** (671 items: HumanEval 164, MBPP 257, GSM8K 250; greedy, thinking off): the community ROCm port
  (bf16) 636, the ROCm port this build started from (bf16) 632, the int8-dense builds 635. Two bf16 builds already
  differ by 4 items: no measurable loss.
- **Agentic benchmark** (the author's, private: a coding agent in OpenCode fixing 29 bugs planted in a ~50k-line
  codebase, long sessions, single runs): builds with the int8 attention KV cache fixed 8-9 bugs, builds with the bf16 KV
  12-14. The int8 KV is out of every profile ([options.md](options.md)).
- **What the agentic benchmark covered**: the two-card builds that scored 12-13 had the uneven split, int8 dense layers,
  one MoE all-reduce per block, the split-K GEMVs, the top-k-first sampler, 16k chunks with blocked PLE, expert reuse in
  prefill, the host-memory all-reduce and the tuned prefill tiles (swept again since, on upstream's rewritten prefill
  GEMM, whose NVFP4 answers differ). Added after the last scored build, and checked for exactness instead: the tuned
  decode tiles, up to 4 concurrent requests (a request's decode is identical alone or batched; prompts prefilled
  together can differ at rounding level), the RAM tier, the sampler rework for requests without a small `top_k`, rank
  0's token broadcast, the MTP head's drafts drawn under each request's sampling (exact speculative sampling) and three
  or four requests verifying 2 rows each on `xtx-xt-4x262k` (greedy answers unchanged). The one-card profiles were not
  run on it. A build on ROCm 10 with the MTP head (`xtx-xt`) scored 12 and 18 in two runs; the same build with the EXL3
  checkpoints ([how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#exl3-checkpoints)) scored 13 at 3.05 bpw and 12 at 4.05 bpw, one run
  each.
- **Exactness checks**: a fixed set of 120 greedy prompts (not published) gave identical answers for the host-memory
  all-reduce, the tuned NVFP4 tiles (prefill and decode), expert reuse in prefill, a single request on the 4-request
  build, and the review-fix branch against the swept one. Kernel checks prove the blocked prefill MoE and batched decode
  rows identical (`moe_block_check.py`, `int8_rows_check.py`); four conversations pushed out to the RAM tier and brought
  back give the same greedy answers (and `host_kv_check.py` checks the copies).

## Images (`--vision`, `xtx-xt`)

Measured with `rdna3/serve.sh --vision`, images capped at 1024 tokens unless stated otherwise.

**Text with the vision build.** Four sessions ran interleaved (text-only, vision, text-only, vision), each with three
`quick_bench.py` runs; the ranges below span both sessions of each mode:

| | text-only | `--vision` |
|---|---:|---:|
| decode, 512 tokens | 53.1-55.1 tok/s | 53.3-54.3 tok/s |
| cold read, 8.3k tokens | 4.28-4.40 s | 4.37-4.40 s |
| agent turn, ~1.5k new tokens | 1.27-1.29 s | 1.27-1.28 s |
| expert cache (both ranks take the smaller plan) | 7,228 | 7,217 |
| greedy answers, 34 prompts of 20 to 20k tokens (thinking off) | reference | identical in every session |

With the tower on both ranks (a first version), rank 1 planned 351 fewer experts (6,877): rank 1 never encodes, so
it holds no tower.

**Depth, two cards.** The depth sweep of this page ran four times, interleaved (text-only, vision, text-only,
vision). Each ran on a fresh server, with the same unseen text for the two modes of a pass and greedy 256-token
answers (`ignore_eos`). The depths land a little below the sweeps above:

| Depth | TG text (2 passes) | TG `--vision` | PP new, text / vision | Agent turn, text / vision |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 9.2k | 55.3 / 55.4 | 54.5 / 54.0 | 1496 / 1505 | 1.27 / 1.27 s |
| 16.6k | 55.3 / 56.5 | 55.8 / 56.2 | 1840 / 1838 | 1.28 / 1.28 s |
| 35.9k | 54.9 / 55.7 | 55.4 / 55.4 | 1902 / 1890 | 1.33 / 1.33 s |
| 73.9k | 55.3 / 56.1 | 52.5 / 55.3 | 1942 / 1944 | 1.44 / 1.44 s |
| 103.2k | 56.5 / 56.2 | 56.0 / 55.0 | 1878 / 1876 | 1.51 / 1.53 s |
| 139.1k | 54.5 / 55.5 | 56.7 / 53.2 | 1811 / 1806 | 1.66 / 1.67 s |
| 166.3k | 56.1 / 56.1 | 56.4 / 54.6 | 1751 / 1756 | 1.74 / 1.72 s |
| 202.9k | 55.4 / 55.3 | 55.1 / 55.1 | 1727 / 1731 | 1.88 / 1.85 s |
| 232.3k | 56.5 / 57.0 | 54.5 / 56.1 | 1676 / 1676 | 1.94 / 1.93 s |
| 253.5k | 54.7 / 55.2 | 54.5 / 54.3 | 1617 / 1606 | 1.98 / 2.00 s |

At the full depth (255.6k tokens), vision was asked about a screenshot at the end of the conversation. It read the
id in both passes (first token in 2.5 s).

**Depth, one card** (`xtx` and `xt`, two passes of each mode, same method, to 124k):

| Depth | `xtx` TG text | `xtx` TG vision | `xtx` PP text / vision | `xt` TG text | `xt` TG vision | `xt` PP text / vision |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8.7k | 35.3 / 35.4 | 34.2 / 34.7 | 731 / 939 | 28.1 / 29.0 | 27.9 / 27.9 | 860 / 879 |
| 16.4k | 43.9 / 35.6 | 34.3 / 34.3 | 1417 / 1412 | 34.2 / 28.1 | 27.5 / 28.0 | 1258 / 1264 |
| 32.8k | 35.2 / 34.3 | 34.8 / 34.6 | 1468 / 1468 | 27.7 / 28.2 | 33.5 / 27.2 | 1340 / 1344 |
| 66.1k | 34.8 / 34.7 | 34.0 / 34.2 | 1452 / 1456 | 28.5 / 37.4 | 27.4 / 28.0 | 1328 / 1328 |
| 97.7k | 35.1 / 37.7 | 40.3 / 43.9 | 1397 / 1408 | 28.7 / 36.8 | 33.9 / 27.3 | 1274 / 1277 |
| 123.2k | 35.3 / 38.7 | 34.9 / 41.8 | 1374 / 1378 | 28.9 / 37.3 | 36.0 / 29.0 | 1248 / 1254 |


On one card the tower sits on the only rank, and the expert cache shrinks by ~165 experts: `xtx` 3,653 -> 3,487
(-4.5 %), `xt` 2,420 -> 2,255 (-6.8 %). That is 436 MiB. Measured with the tower alone, the streamed weights and
their staging take 130 MiB, and the first encode takes ~170 MiB more outside PyTorch's allocator (94 MiB of it for
the patch embedding's Conv3d, in MIOpen). Decode loses ~1.5-2 % outside the steps where both modes jump (35-44 tok/s on
the XTX, 33-37 on the XT, depending on the generated text): `xtx` ~35.2 -> ~34.5 tok/s, `xt` ~28.4 -> ~27.8 tok/s.
Prompt reading is unchanged, and the agent turn is 0-1.5 % longer. The screenshot at 125.3k was read in all four vision
passes (first token in 3.2-3.3 s).

**The tower alone** (`rdna3/bench/vision_tower_bench.py`; one card, weights streamed from RAM, seeded random pixels):

| image tokens | pixels | XTX | XT | peak VRAM beyond the weights |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 256 | 0.3 MP | 33 ms | 33 ms | 25 MiB |
| 1024 | 1.0 MP | 91 ms | 107 ms | 97 MiB |
| 2048 | 2.1 MP | 268 ms | 307 ms | 142 MiB |
| 4096 | 4.2 MP | 871 ms | 1012 ms | 253 MiB |
| 8192 | 8.4 MP | 3.2 s | 3.8 s | 371 MiB |
| 16384 | 16.8 MP | 12.1 s | 15.0 s | 742 MiB |

- **Attention memory is linear.** PyTorch's attention runs its AOTriton kernel (`attn_fwd`) on gfx1100, so memory
  grows linearly with the image; nothing ran out of memory up to 16384 tokens.
- **Weight placement.** Streaming the weights from RAM leaves 294 MiB of them in VRAM; keeping them all resident
  (`--mm-encoder-weights gpu`) takes 1034 MiB and gains nothing (106 against 107 ms at 1024 tokens on the XT).
- **Both cards agree.** The XTX and the XT gave bit-identical embeddings at nine sizes from 64 to 8192 tokens.

**Requests** (thinking off, 16 to 120 output tokens):

- **Small print.** A 1920x1080 screenshot of 30 lines of 16-pixel text becomes 1055 prompt tokens at the 1024 cap. 3
  ids of 3 were read, in 1.6 s; at a 2048 cap it was 2087 tokens, 1.9 s, same answers.
- **Concurrent requests.** Four sampled image requests at once were all correct, with 0 rank disagreements under
  `FREETOKEN_TP_SYNC_TOKENS=check`.
- **Repeated image and follow-up turn.** The same image twice in one prompt was answered correctly. A follow-up turn
  reused the cached image prefix (2048 cached tokens, 52 new).
- **Latency.** The first image request after a start took 3.7 s; later ones took 1.8-2.0 s for a 1034-token prompt.
  The first request of any kind after a start takes 1.3-1.9 s, the JIT modules being kept in the kernel-cache volume.

## Memory while serving (`xtx-xt`)

| | Used (MTP head on) |
|---|---|
| XTX VRAM | ~21.3 GiB of 24.0 while decoding (the desktop's share included), up to ~23.7 GiB while a 16k-token chunk is read deep in the context |
| XT VRAM | ~18.0 GiB of 20.0 while decoding, up to ~19.9 GiB while a 16k-token chunk is read deep in the context |
| Host RAM | 82 GiB resident over the two processes, all of it locked (`FREETOKEN_MLOCK`): ~63 GiB of experts (each rank pins its own share of every expert), the RAM tier (4.6 + 4.9 GiB with the snapshots), the rest the processes |

VRAM is the driver's count (`mem_info_vram_used`) sampled twice a second over a depth sweep to 248k: the ~2 GiB left
free per card while decoding is the prefill's working memory, which a deep 16k-token chunk uses almost entirely (56 MiB
left on the XT). Host RAM is the kernel's `Mlocked` count after start.

**Every profile and checkpoint** (one server each, `rdna3/serve.sh`): RAM is the growth of the kernel's `Mlocked`
count from before the start to after it, and the expert cache the planned size, of 24,576 experts (the same on both
cards: each rank plans on its own free memory, then both take the smaller plan), both from the servers of the summary
above (`xtx-xt` at 262,144 tokens of context; an earlier build: a later one locks 1.2 GiB more RAM and caches 7 % more
experts with NVFP4, 6,977 -> 7,464 slots); VRAM, from an earlier build, is the highest `mem_info_vram_used` sampled
every 50 ms over an agent-like first turn (a title request decoding while a ~21k-token prompt is read), the decode
answers, `quick_bench.py` and the depth sweep, the desktop's share included.

| | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| RAM locked, `xtx-xt` / `xtx` / `xt` | 82 / 73 / 73 GiB | 60 / 51 / 51 GiB | 75 / 66 / 66 GiB |
| Expert cache, `xtx-xt` / `xtx` / `xt` | 6,990 / 3,567 / 2,328 | 9,800 / 4,902 / 3,057 | 7,217 / 3,686 / 2,298 |
| VRAM peak, `xtx-xt` (XTX / XT of 24,560 / 20,464 MiB) | 23,524 / 20,291 MiB | 24,284 / 19,228 MiB | 24,035 / 19,197 MiB |
| VRAM peak, `xtx` / `xt` | 23,506 / 19,367 MiB | 22,943 / 19,072 MiB | 22,868 / 19,081 MiB |

No GPU queue was stopped by a full VRAM in those VRAM runs; the two 4.05 bpw one-card servers stopped their queues
once, for 47-59 ms, on their first request (the VRAM was 1.7 GiB from full; the cause was not traced).

How to reproduce or check a change: [testing.md](testing.md).


---

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/how-it-works.md -->

# How it works

What this build changes in FreeToken, and why, for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on RDNA3. Upstream's own design (expert
offload, radix cache, FTW weights, APIs) is described in [FREETOKEN_UPSTREAM_README.md](../FREETOKEN_UPSTREAM_README.md).

## The problem

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 48 layers (12 attention "QSA" layers + 36 GatedDeltaNet (GDN) linear-attention layers), 512
experts per layer (24,576 in all), ~6B parameters active per token, per-layer n-gram embeddings (PLE),
hyper-connections, 262k context. In NVFP4 the experts alone are 68 GB and the n-gram tables 51 GB, against 44 GB of
VRAM on an XTX + XT. The two cards cannot read each other's memory (no GPU peer-to-peer on the reference machine, as
usual on consumer boards): every exchange between them goes through system RAM.

## Where everything lives

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| GPU VRAM | dense weights (int8) except the input embedding, the KV cache of the attention layers, the GDN recurrent states, and an **expert cache** filling everything else (on `xtx-xt`: 7.5k of the 24,576 experts, on each card) |
| System RAM | **every expert** (~63 GiB, pinned; each rank holds its own share of every expert), the input embedding (1.2 GiB, a row per token read across PCIe), the PLE rows prefills read (a RAM cache, 0.12-0.17 GiB), conversations moved off the GPUs (the RAM tier), the ranks' exchange buffer |
| Disk | the n-gram embedding tables, read row by row on demand (direct I/O, no page cache; a large fill over four io_uring rings) |

## One decode step

For each token, on both cards at once (tensor parallel): the dense projections (int8 GEMVs), then in each MoE layer
the router picks the experts, the ones in the GPU cache are used in place and the missing ones are copied from RAM over
PCIe (a least-recently-used cache), then an all-reduce joins the two halves of the layer, then sampling. Profiling
the untuned build: the GPUs were busy 99 % of the step; 53-56 % of it went to bf16 dense GEMMs running at ~20 % of VRAM
bandwidth, 14 % to PCIe expert copies, 7-14 % to all-reduces (the XTX waiting for the XT). The work below attacks those
three shares.

## Dense layers: int8 weights (+28 % decode)

The checkpoint keeps every non-expert tensor in bf16. At load, each dense linear layer is converted to int8 weights
with one scale per output channel and rank (routers stay bf16), and decode uses Triton GEMVs written for RDNA3 (2D
accumulator, one reduction, fused scale). Half the bytes per token, and ~2.4 GiB per card freed for the expert cache.
This is lossy (8-bit weights): no measurable loss on the scored benchmark, and it was in the builds validated on the
agentic one. The allocator is compacted after the conversion, or the freed memory stays fragmented and is lost.
Several concurrent requests run the same per-row kernel once per row, so a request's decode gets the same bits alone
or batched.

## Two unequal cards: uneven tensor parallelism (+4 %)

Upstream serves Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on one GPU only (its loader and NVFP4 expert kernels refuse TP>1) and refuses TP
ranks whose free memory differs by more than 2 GiB. This build's tensor-parallel port splits evenly by default. With
`FREETOKEN_TP_ALLOW_IMBALANCE` the memory plan uses the smaller card, and with `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.55` the experts'
intermediate dimension (routed and shared) is split 55 / 45 (60 / 40 with an EXL3 checkpoint, whose slices must be
whole 128-wide blocks) and the GDN heads 9 / 7 (key) and 27 / 21 (value): the XTX has 20 % more VRAM and
~14 % more compute, so both finish together, and the XT's smaller share of each expert lets both cards cache more
experts (the ranks all use the smallest card's plan). Attention stays even (2 KV heads cannot be split unevenly). The
input embedding stays even; the LM head's rows follow the same shares with `FREETOKEN_LMHEAD_SPLIT` (on in the two-card
profiles: each logit is one rank's dot product, so its bits do not depend on the split); the hyper-connection
mixers, the PLE projections, the attention indexer, the norms and the routers are replicated; with
`--ple-backend disk` (every profile) each rank reads every PLE head from disk, hashed on the host.

## Talking between the cards: host-memory all-reduce (+2.5-4.8 %)

Without peer-to-peer, RCCL stages each small decode all-reduce (5 KB) through host memory with its proxy threads:
~12 µs inside a CUDA graph, ~97 times per token. Here both ranks map one shared host-memory region and a one-block
kernel copies, signals, waits and adds (fp32, rounded to bf16 exactly as RCCL does): 6 µs, same bits. Separately, the
two MoE all-reduces of a layer (routed and shared experts) are merged into one (+2.7 % decode): that change reorders
sums and was validated on the agentic benchmark.

## The expert cache

Upstream's LRU cache over the GPU memory left after weights and KV (`--moe-cache-auto`). Policies were compared on
real traces: LFU = LRU, and even the offline optimum (Belady) only halves the misses; capacity, not policy, is the
lever, which is why every freed megabyte goes to the cache. Expert GEMM tiles were re-swept for this model on these
cards, changing only tiles that keep the summation order (bit-exact).

## Prefill

A prefill chunk runs every token through every layer, so a long chunk streams all 512 experts of every layer over PCIe
(~700 MB per layer per card). What this build does about it ([benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md) has the current speeds):

- **Big chunks.** 16k-token chunks on two cards, 8k on one (its working memory is smaller): each chunk streams the
  experts once, so in the A/B test an 8.4k prompt read in 4.3 s instead of 5.5 s with 4k chunks, and 54-101k-token
  reads at depth 2-6 % faster. To fit, the MoE and the PLE layer run 4096 tokens at a time inside the chunk (the NVFP4
  MoE 8192 in `xtx-xt` and `xtx-xt-4x262k`). The NVFP4 MoE blocks are bit-identical (an EXL3 block of 25 tokens or
  fewer rounds differently: [options.md](options.md#experts-moe)); the PLE blocks can round differently, checked to
  tolerance and validated on the agentic benchmark for one request.
- **Experts already on the GPU** are gathered there instead of crossing PCIe again (`--moe-prefill-hit-d2d`, with
  `hipMemcpyBatchAsync` on ROCm, or one copy per entry on older HIP): a third of the experts stay off PCIe per chunk.
- **The all-reduces overlap the compute** on two cards: each block of a chunk's routed experts and of its
  GatedDeltaNet output starts its all-reduce while the next block computes (the same bits).
- **The per-layer-embedding rows come from disk** without stopping the GPUs: rank 0 alone reads them, on a thread,
  over four io_uring rings, and broadcasts them; while a chunk computes, the next chunk's rows are read (they took
  ~1.1 s per 16k-token chunk with the GPUs idle). The rows read before stay in a RAM cache, since an agent session's
  n-grams recur across its turns.
- **Kernels shaped for RDNA3**, all with the same bits: the QSA indexer scores 16 query rows a program, a long expert
  block runs its full tiles in one launch and its remaining rows in smaller tiles in a second, and kernels that
  spilled registers run more warps.
- **The input embedding lives in RAM**, a row per token read across PCIe, and its VRAM goes to the expert cache.

The PLE reads on a thread, the all-reduce overlap and the indexer's 16 rows together made fully cold reads ~25 %
shorter ([journey.md](journey.md#33-short-turns-the-host-waiting-at-every-layer-2026-10-18-and-19)).

### Short chunks: agent turns

A short chunk (up to 1280 tokens on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, typically an agent's tool result) routes to only part of the
experts, so it does not stream whole layers:

- **It reads its routed experts through the expert cache**, and only the missing ones cross PCIe. The next layer's
  experts are predicted by that layer's router applied to this layer's input, and copied while this one computes;
  with NVFP4, whose short turns keep PCIe saturated, only the experts at least two tokens predict are copied ahead.
  The same bits: the GEMM tiles follow the expert ids.
- **With the K/V in host RAM** it copies to VRAM only the K/V rows its tokens select.
- **The tokenizer reuses the previous prompt's tokens** instead of encoding the whole conversation again.
- **The host keeps the GPU busy**: the predicted experts' copy plan is read once the layer's GEMMs are queued (not in a
  sync at every layer), Triton kernels launch through a shorter host path, the int8 weights are dequantized in one
  pass, and the expert tiles are sized for a few rows an expert.

On `xtx-xt-4x262k`, a ~520-token agent turn at 45k of context takes ~0.49 s to its first token with EXL3 3.05 bpw and
0.71-0.73 s with NVFP4 (three 262k contexts); a 142-360-token turn at 224k took 0.46-0.59 s with EXL3 on an earlier build.
How each step was measured: [journey.md](journey.md#27-agent-turns-short-prefills-through-the-expert-cache-2026-10-14),
[section 31](journey.md#31-short-agent-turns-2026-10-17-and-18) and
[section 33](journey.md#33-short-turns-the-host-waiting-at-every-layer-2026-10-18-and-19).

## Sampling on ROCm

Upstream's exact top-k / top-p kernels coordinate several blocks per row with a spin barrier that needs every block
of the row running at once; the cooperative launch does not give that on this ROCm stack, and they hang on gfx1100.
Here:

- when every request of a batch has a small `top_k` (the model's default is 20), the batch samples from its top-k
  candidates: one `torch.topk`, then one small kernel does temperature, softmax, top-p and the draw (~0.07 ms);
- otherwise an exact threshold comes from a sort of the probabilities (top-k = the k-th largest value, top-p = the
  largest value whose cumulative mass reaches p), and the draw uses upstream's multi-block inverse-CDF kernels, which
  need no barrier: 0.2 ms for one request, 1 ms for four, on any distribution (upstream's kernels with one block per
  row took 10 ms on a peaked row and 33-60 ms on a flat one);
- every rank samples its own copy of the logits, and rank 0's tokens are broadcast after each sampled step, so two
  different GPUs can never drift onto different tokens;
- with the MTP head on two cards (`FREETOKEN_SPARSE_LOGITS`, on in the two-card profiles), a decode step needs only
  each row's top-k: each rank takes the k largest of its half of the logits, the ranks exchange those (2k floats a row
  instead of the half vocabulary) and a kernel merges them back into `torch.topk`'s values, ids and order (equal bf16
  logits are frequent, and topk orders them differently for one row and for several: both reproduced); the verify
  step's speculative sampling and each draft's draw then run as one Triton kernel each, written to give the torch
  ops' bits (`FREETOKEN_SAMPLE_KERNELS`). Greedy and sampled answers are identical to the whole-vocabulary path.

The sorted path is checked by kernel tests (same kept sets as the float64 definition, seeded draws identical to
upstream's kernels), the broadcast by `FREETOKEN_TP_SYNC_TOKENS=check` server runs (0 disagreements over ~8k sampled
tokens); neither was run on the agentic benchmark. Why not the older vendored sampling module:
[decisions.md](decisions.md#sampling-on-rocm).

## Several requests at once

Up to 4 requests decode together (`--max-running-requests 4`), with CUDA graphs captured for every batch size up to 4.
The decode GEMVs run their unchanged per-row body once per request (the weight tile loaded once when the reduction fits
one tile), so batching changes the speed of a request's decode, not its tokens. Prompts prefilled in the same forward can differ at rounding level (the dense GEMMs run at
another size), as prefix caching already makes them. A request alone gives the same answers as with one request at a
time (120 prompts); batched runs were not run on the agentic benchmark. Prefills are not mixed with
decode steps in one batch (estimated at ~3 %, not done); agents naturally overlap their prefills.

## Conversations kept in RAM

Upstream's hybrid radix cache keeps, per conversation prefix, the attention KV pages and a snapshot of the GDN
recurrent state at the end of the last prompt; a returning conversation resumes from there. When the GPU pool is full
it evicts the least recently used prefixes, and their conversations are re-read from scratch (~45-55 s for 100k
tokens). With `FREETOKEN_HOST_KV=1` an evicted node is **demoted** instead: its KV pages and GDN snapshot are copied to
pinned RAM and the node stays in the tree; a later match **promotes** it back (fresh GPU pages and state slot,
host-to-device copies, ~20 GB/s). The copies are exact. Eviction splits a node when only part of it has to leave (an
agent turn is one node), capacities are counted in pages and snapshots so both ranks take identical decisions, and
nodes being promoted are pinned against eviction. It pays when conversations together outgrow the GPU pool, as
parallel sub-agents do; a single conversation that fits the GPUs gains nothing, and the tier's RAM stays locked for
the whole run ([options.md](options.md#conversations-kept-in-ram)).

## Images (`--vision`, off by default)

The Qwen3.8 vision tower (27 ViT blocks, ~0.45 B parameters) is upstream's, and it was never split across the GPUs.

- **Where the tower runs.** Rank 0 builds it whole and encodes every image. The embeddings are broadcast to the
  other rank (5 MiB for a 1024-token image), so both ranks put the same numbers in their residual stream. Rank 1
  holds no tower, and its expert cache keeps the room.
- **Weights.** The tower's blocks stream from pinned RAM two at a time, and the tower stays bf16 under
  `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE`.
- **Positions.** The text model switches to the 3-axis rope (mrope) that the image positions need. For text it gives
  the same rotation: greedy answers are identical, and speed is the same up to 255k of context on two cards.

Numbers: [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#images---vision-xtx-xt).

## EXL3 checkpoints

[exllamav3](https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3)'s EXL3 format is read directly: a variant of QTIP where each
16x16 tile of a weight is a tail-biting trellis of K bits per weight, decoded through a procedural codebook, between
two 128-point Hadamard rotations with per-channel scales (`W = diag(suh) H Wq H diag(svh)`). Nothing to switch on: a
checkpoint whose `quantization_config` says `quant_method: exl3` selects it, e.g. `turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3`,
branch `3.05bpw_h5_ng5` (routed experts at 3 bits per weight, most other linears at 5, the n-gram table at 5).

- **Routed experts stay EXL3**, in the host banks and in the GPU cache: 1.86 MB per expert against 2.76 MB in NVFP4.
  Triton kernels written for gfx1100 decode the trellis in registers (the byte sum of the `mul1` codebook is one
  `v_dot4_u32_u8`): split-K GEMVs in decode, a grouped GEMM over expert-sorted tokens in prefill, and the Hadamard
  rotations around them. Every expert has its own input scales, so the input is rotated once per routed expert.
- **Every other linear** (attention, GDN, shared expert, LM head, MTP head, vision tower) is decoded to bf16 on the
  GPU as it loads (a few seconds), then follows the usual path: `FREETOKEN_INT8_DENSE=1` converts it to int8 as for
  NVFP4 (the vision tower stays bf16, as it does with NVFP4). exllamav3 zero-pads a linear to 128-multiples (the
  vision MLP: 4304 -> 4352); the loader cuts it back. Codebook markers are looked up in every file of the checkpoint,
  the index and the files beside it (4.05 bpw keeps its vision tower in `vision_k6.safetensors`); a linear without a
  marker is 3inst, as in exllamav3.
- **The n-gram table** (one 160-wide 5-bit trellis ring per row and a bias per hash head: 33 GB instead of 51 GB) is
  read by the disk PLE backend (`--ple-backend disk`, the profiles' setting) and decoded on the GPU after each fill.
- **The MTP head's experts** are EXL3 too and join the bank as they are.
- A card's slice of the 640-wide expert intermediate must be whole 128-wide Hadamard blocks: two cards get 384 / 256
  (`FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.55` rounds to that), the shared expert too; an even split (320 / 320) is refused at start, so
  the profiles of two equal cards (`xtx-xtx`, `xt-xt`) need `FREETOKEN_TP_SPLIT=0.6` in their file (untested).
- Prefill rotates the inputs in one kernel, runs the gate|up GEMM, the step between the products, then the down GEMM
  with the rotation out, the scales and the router weight as its epilogue (a program owns a 128-column block), and a
  plain per-token sum.
- **Prefill temporaries are kept out of the cache.** A 4096-token block holds the rotated inputs of both projections
  per route (fp16) and the gate|up products (fp32): 0.61 GiB on the 384-wide slice, 0.57 on the 256-wide one, for a
  16k-token chunk, more than the generic `(1 - memory_ratio)` headroom absorbs. The expert kernel declares them
  (`prefill_workspace_bytes`) and the cache planner leaves them free (`MoE prefill temporaries` in the start log; 5 %
  fewer cached experts). Without that, the first 16k-token prefill after a start filled the 7900 XTX; on two cards
  `rdna3/serve.sh` also lowers `--memory-ratio` to 0.77 (0.76 from 4 bpw): see
  [journey.md](journey.md#16-exl3-checkpoints-2026-10-04).
- Not supported: half-integer bitrates, mixed expert bitrates across layers, the pinned PLE backend, the encoder-only
  weight reader (the CPU expert executor of `--hybrid` does read EXL3 experts: [cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)). FTW conversion is untested. The vision tower reads the checkpoint's bf16
  `qkv` (image input checked with one image per branch).

Measured with an earlier build (this one reads faster, caches more experts and locks 1.2 GiB more RAM: [CHANGELOG.md](../../CHANGELOG.md)), with the profiles' settings, MTP head on, one request (decode: greedy, from 9k tokens to the profile's maximum context;
RAM: locked while serving;
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#depth-sweep-exl3-checkpoints) has every step, the cold reads and the sampled decode):

| | NVFP4 | EXL3 3.05 bpw | EXL3 4.05 bpw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| download | 135 GB | 85 GB | 108 GB |
| experts in RAM (without the MTP head's) | 63.3 GiB | 42.6 GiB | 56.7 GiB |
| decode, `xtx-xt` / `xtx` / `xt` | 78-96 / 36-44 / 29-34 tok/s | 95-117 / 52-58 / 41-46 tok/s | 86-94 / 37-47 / 29-36 tok/s |
| reading a new block, `xtx-xt` | 1910-2180 tok/s | 1940-2280 tok/s | 1970-2270 tok/s |
| agent turn, first token, `xtx-xt` | 0.8-0.9 s | 0.7-0.9 s | 0.8-1.0 s |
| RAM locked, `xtx-xt` / one card | 82 / 73 GiB | 60 / 51 GiB | 75 / 66 GiB |
| expert cache per card, `xtx-xt` | 7.0k | 9.8k | 7.2k |
| agentic benchmark (29 bugs) | 12 and 18 (two runs) | 13 (one run) | 12 (one run) |

The agentic benchmark scores come from earlier builds than the other rows. The checkpoints answer differently, so the MTP head
keeps a different share of its guesses: compare decode rates as an order of magnitude. Greedy answers are identical
with and without the head. With the RAM tier off and `--expert-load serial`, the 3.05 bpw server started and served under a
56 GiB container limit at 52.3 GiB used (`quick_bench.py` then: 70.1 tok/s decode at the model's sampling, 8.3k-token
cold read in 4.41 s, agent turn 0.89 s, tool call parsed); a real 64 GB machine is untested.

## What stays upstream's

The HTTP APIs and parsers and the FTW format are upstream's. The scheduler, the radix cache, the offload engine and the
qwen4_exp loader are upstream's with this build's hooks (RAM tier, GDN boundary carry, relay handshake, tensor-parallel
sharding, expert reuse in prefill on ROCm, tuned and blocked NVFP4 kernels); every changed file is listed in [changes-from-upstream.md](changes-from-upstream.md).

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/decisions.md -->

# Decisions and trade-offs

The main choices behind this build, what they cost, and the measurement that settled each one. The story in order is
in [journey.md](journey.md); the options themselves in [options.md](options.md).

## Rule 0: precision before speed
