<!-- file: docs/rdna3/maintaining.md -->

# Maintaining

How this repository relates to upstream FreeToken and how to keep it current. For maintainers.

## What this tree is

Upstream [FlashML-org/FreeToken](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken) at `cc56b6b` ("feat(gguf): serve
GLM-5.3-Flash GGUF checkpoints on glm5-next (#721)"), plus the changes listed file by file in
[changes-from-upstream.md](changes-from-upstream.md). The history is upstream's own up to `0d652e7`, then this
project's commits on top (the first one holds everything up to 0.1.0), a merge of upstream up
to `ee9789f`, five upstream commits cherry-picked (`74a3877`, `9c635a1`, `7d6490c`, `9b68e00`, `b6193e8`, authors
kept), a merge of the rest up to `9b68e00` and a merge up to `cc56b6b`. Once the `upstream` remote is set up (below),
`git diff $(git merge-base HEAD upstream/main)` shows every change against the upstream version this tree is based on.

## The stack on top of upstream (oldest first)

| Piece | Origin | Leaves the stack when |
|---|---|---|
| RCCL for tensor-parallel execution | upstream PR #135 (zihaomu) | #135 merges |
| LDS clamp of the QSA attend kernel for RDNA's 64 KiB | community ROCm port (lukascechovic), upstream issue #349 | upstream's clamp (`7d6490c`, #587) sizes the tiles with the K/V cache's itemsize, this one with q's (the same tile unless K/V is 1 byte): kept ahead of it until they agree |
| TP>1 relay handshake before the first request | community ROCm port (lukascechovic), upstream issue #364 | upstream fixes #364 |
| GDN boundary carried across the prefill chunk seam | community ROCm port (lukascechovic) | upstream carries it |
| qwen4_exp tensor parallelism | rewritten from the community port's | upstream supports qwen4_exp at TP>1 |
| unequal cards, uneven split, int8 dense, GEMVs, host all-reduce, sampler, tuned tiles, blocked prefill, multi-request, RAM tier, review fixes | this repository | upstream merges it (to be proposed piece by piece) |
| MTP head, EXL3 checkpoints, K/V in host RAM, short prefills through the expert cache, `--hybrid` on ROCm | this repository | upstream merges it |
| `kernel/triton/moe_align.py` on ROCm, over upstream's staged align (`0bca88f`) | this repository (Triton 3.8 histogram fix) | upstream's align is checked on ROCm's Triton 3.8, or Triton fixes the histogram range |
| hybrid publish / merge kernels over pinned flag words | this repository | upstream drops its copies around the doorbell on ROCm |
| HIP stream memops for the PLE wait-sync (`row_store_ext.cpp`) | this repository | upstream's row store finds HIP's memops |
| `LaunchKernel::with_attr` refuses `use_pdl=True` on ROCm | this repository | upstream refuses it too |
| `Dockerfile.rdna3`, `rdna3/`, `docs/rdna3/` | this repository | never |

Left the stack at the merge of `ee9789f`: upstream merged #134 (CUDA-only backends gated off on ROCm, `9b585b7`) and
carries #133's HIP-portable JIT kernels since `803a3b4` (#133 itself was closed). Of both, this tree keeps one line: on
ROCm, `LaunchKernel::with_attr` refuses `use_pdl=True` where upstream ignores it. The YaRN rope table and the split
top-k past 16 chunks, written here first, are upstream's own since `235e201` and `5031e3d`.

At the merge of `9b68e00`: upstream's vendored ggml-cuda kernels (`e5d3bd3`, they build for gfx1100)
replaced this tree's ROCm build of the old GGUF kernels; upstream's hybrid ensure kernel splits the routes (`f02fbb1`),
which this tree's split kernel did, and its executor speaks HIP's memops (`2010271`), which this tree added: both left
the stack. Kept over upstream: `kernel/triton/moe_align.py` on ROCm instead of the staged align of `0bca88f` (the same
Triton 3.8 bug, fixed in the kernel here); the hybrid publish / merge kernels instead of upstream's copies around the
doorbell, which it keeps on ROCm. The prefill through the slot cache needs one slot pool (`b416f85`'s default here).

At the merge of `cc56b6b`: upstream's CPU MoE executor serves a format per MoE layer (`e8c6bf1`) and computes GGUF
experts with ggml-cpu instead of its Q4_0 kernels (`c8559fd`); this tree's EXL3 experts (with their own fp16 decode,
which upstream dropped from the shared header in `0db5023`), route grouping and hybrid flag words sit on it, and
`FREETOKEN_HYBRID_FETCH_FRACTION` fills its per-layer fractions. Upstream moved the NVFP4 launches to
`kernel/nvfp4_moe.py` (`ac6a15d`) and rewrote the Triton prefill GEMM (`03c2c9c`): the RDNA3 decode tiles and the skip
of the CPU's routes moved with the launches, the RDNA3 prefill tiles were swept again on the new GEMM. NVFP4 global
scales are fp32 (`0db5023`); with the rewritten GEMM, NVFP4 answers differ from the build before, EXL3 ones do not. The
qwen4_exp dense reader is upstream's scheme-driven one (`163d1de`), with this tree's tensor-parallel sharding, EXL3
reconstruction and MTP head on top; the expert-piece hook takes upstream's `layers` argument, and the TP slicing keeps
the experts' static activation scales (`e4f69d9`) whole on every rank.

## Keeping current

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken.git     # once
git remote add luka https://github.com/lukascechovic/FreeToken.git       # optional: the community ROCm port
rdna3/tools/upstream-status.sh        # read-only: new upstream commits, and which stack pieces they touch
git checkout -b sync-upstream && git merge upstream/main              # on a branch, merged into main once validated
```

Upstream is merged, not rebased onto: the published history is never rewritten, so clones and forks keep working.
To take only some upstream commits, `git cherry-pick -x <commit>` keeps their author and records where they came
from; `upstream-status.sh` leaves the commits so recorded out of the new ones.
`upstream-status.sh` also reads an optional `luka` remote (the community ROCm port) when it exists. When upstream lands
one of the pieces of the table above, resolve the conflict in upstream's favour, then update the table and
[changes-from-upstream.md](changes-from-upstream.md).

After a merge, update the base commit named in `NOTICE`, this file and
[changes-from-upstream.md](changes-from-upstream.md), and its line counts
(`git diff --numstat $(git merge-base HEAD upstream/main)`). Then, in this order, each step gating the next:

1. CPU tests ([testing.md](testing.md)): only the environment failures listed there.
2. `docker build -f Dockerfile.rdna3 -t freetoken-rdna3:<tag> .` (its content checks must pass).
3. GPU validation ([testing.md](testing.md), the procedure): smoke test with sampling and a tool call, greedy answers
   identical to the previous build, decode / prefill windows interleaved against it, the depth sweep, several agents.
4. Release only if speed is at least equal and every check passes; keep the previous image as a fallback.

## Releasing

1. Measure on the image being released, then update every place the numbers appear: [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md),
   `README.md`, `llms.txt`, [profiles.md](profiles.md), the headers in `rdna3/profiles/`, the banner
   (`docs/rdna3/assets/social-preview.png`, rendered from `social-preview.html`) and `CHANGELOG.md`; then run
   `rdna3/tools/make-llms-full.sh`. `rdna3/bench/quick_bench.py` and `depth_sweep.py` take the headline numbers.
2. `rdna3/tools/privacy_scan.sh` (machine names as extra patterns): no personal paths, e-mail addresses, secrets or AI co-author lines in the
   tree or the history being published.
3. Tag the release `rdna3-vX.Y.Z` (upstream's own tags are `vX.Y.Z`, so a fetch from upstream never clashes), with
   an annotated tag; the image records the commit it was built from (`/opt/FreeToken-BUILD-PROVENANCE.txt`).

## Tuned tiles

The NVFP4 tile tables (`FREETOKEN_NVFP4_*_TUNED`) were produced with `rdna3/bench/nvfp4_*_sweep.py`; rerun them for a
new model, split or card, keeping only tiles that preserve the summation order (M / N tiles, warps, stages). The EXL3
decode GEMV table (`_GEMV_TUNED` in `kernel/triton/exl3.py`) came from `rdna3/bench/exl3_gemv_bench.py` and is keyed
to this model's 384 / 256 shapes; there the N tiles per program keep the sums, the K tile and split change them, and
some warp counts do too (check the outputs bit for bit). The int8 GEMV configs (`_CONFIGS` in
`kernel/triton/int8_gemv.py`): only BLOCK_N keeps the sums; the K block, split and warps change them (checked on the
uneven split's shapes). Sweep cold (48 distinct matrices or 48 layers' own slots, as a decode step reads
them) with a warm-up pass, and time the current config first and last: a warm microbenchmark keeps the weights in the
Infinity Cache and promises gains that serving does not see.


---

# Changes from upstream

This repository is a modified version of [FlashML-org/FreeToken](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken) (Apache
License 2.0), taken at `0d652e7` and merged with upstream up to `ee9789f`, then up to `9b68e00` (five of its commits
cherry-picked first, then the rest merged), then up to `cc56b6b`. Every file changed or added relative to upstream is
listed here with the reason. Line counts are `added/removed`, against the upstream commit a section or row names,
`0d652e7` otherwise; `git diff cc56b6b` gives the current ones. Files the merge made
identical to upstream again are gone from the tables ([maintaining.md](maintaining.md#the-stack-on-top-of-upstream-oldest-first)).
Who wrote what: [credits.md](credits.md).

## ROCm portability (upstream PRs #133-#135 by zihaomu, and fixes on top)

| File | Lines | Change |
|---|---:|---|
| `python/freetoken/kernel/backend.py` | 2/2 against `ee9789f` | the module docstring (the gating itself is upstream's #134, `9b585b7`) |
| `python/freetoken/kernel/csrc/include/freetoken/utils.cuh` | 1/1 against `ee9789f` | on ROCm, `with_attr` refuses `use_pdl=True` (upstream ignores it); the HIP-portable JIT kernels are upstream's (`803a3b4`) |
| `python/freetoken/kernel/pynccl.py` | 7/1 | tensor parallelism routed to RCCL on ROCm |
| `python/freetoken/kernel/triton/qsa/attend.py` | 51/3 | BLOCK_N clamped to RDNA's 64 KiB LDS, sized with q's itemsize (upstream's own clamp, `7d6490c`, sized with the K/V cache's, runs after it and changes no tile; alone it would keep 64 with 1-byte K/V); int8 K/V path (off, not recommended) |
| `tests/engine/test_rocm_communication.py`, `tests/kernels/test_backend.py`, `tests/kernels/test_jit_index_store.py` | new | tests of the above |

## Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4_exp) on several GPUs

| File | Lines | Change |
|---|---:|---|
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/weight.py` | 203/11 | per-rank sharding of the split weights (even or uneven split; the rest, the vision tower included, replicated), ahead of upstream's scheme-driven dense reader (`163d1de`) |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen3_vl/vision.py` | 18/23 | the Qwen VL vision tower never split (whole on a rank) instead of tensor-parallel modules whose weights nothing sharded; a rank without a tower places nothing |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/model.py` | 3/1 | the vision tower built on rank 0 only (rank 0 encodes for every rank) |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/attention.py` | 20/7 | attention heads and output projection sharded |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/gdn.py` | 41/14 | GatedDeltaNet heads sharded, unevenly when a split is set |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/moe.py` | 30/2 | routed / shared experts sharded; one all-reduce per MoE block |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/ple.py` | 106/3 | PLE heads sharded (except with the disk source, which serves every head to every rank); the PLE convolution processed in time blocks for long and batched prefills |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen4_exp/ple_disk.py` | 4/0 | the disk source declares that it serves every PLE head, so each rank reads them all |
| `python/freetoken/layers/quantization/moe/nvfp4.py`, `layers/quantization/moe/base.py` | 60/3, 14/1 | NVFP4 expert banks sliced per rank, unevenly when a split is set |
| `python/freetoken/models/qwen3_5_moe/moe.py` | 7/3 | `_SharedExpert` accepts a rank-local width (used by qwen4_exp's uneven split) |
| `python/freetoken/layers/linear.py`, `layers/moe.py` | 14/4, 4/1 | uneven shard sizes; the fused MoE all-reduce |
| `python/freetoken/kvcache/linear_state_pool.py` | 10/3 | GDN state pool sized per rank |
| `tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_tp_shard.py`, `test_tp_uneven.py`, `test_ple_conv_blocks.py`, `test_ple.py` | new / 2/1 | sharding, uneven split and blocked PLE tests; the snapshot test compares with a tolerance |
| `tests/models/qwen4_exp/common.py` | 16/2 | `as_rank()`: run a test block as one rank of a TP group; `meta_state_dict(vision=True)` |

| `python/freetoken/engine/engine.py` | 30/0 | the process's memory locked once loaded (`FREETOKEN_MLOCK`) so that, with `vm.compact_unevictable_allowed=0`, memory compaction leaves the pages the GPU driver maps alone; a warning while it is 1 |

## EXL3 checkpoints

Line counts here are on top of the lines listed in the sections above.

| File | Lines | Change |
|---|---:|---|
| `python/freetoken/layers/quantization/exl3_codec.py` | new | the EXL3 format in plain torch (trellis rings, codebooks, tile order, Hadamard reconstruction, n-gram rings): the reference the kernels are checked against |
| `python/freetoken/kernel/triton/exl3.py` | new | gfx1100 Triton kernels: tile dequant, split-K decode GEMV, grouped prefill GEMM, Hadamard rotations, n-gram row decode |
| `python/freetoken/layers/quantization/configs/exl3.py`, `configs/__init__.py`, `configs/base.py` | new, 4/3, 6/1 | the `exl3` dialect: routed experts stay EXL3 (bitrate read from the checkpoint), every other linear unquantized; dialects can see the checkpoint path |
| `python/freetoken/layers/quantization/scheme.py`, `moe/exl3.py`, `moe/__init__.py` | 17/0, new, 4/3 | the EXL3 kind and expert method: bank layout, per-rank slicing on 128-blocks, forward |

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/long-context.md -->

# Long contexts: the K/V in host RAM

Two independent settings decide how much context a server holds:

1. **Where the attention K/V lives** sets how many tokens all the requests hold together. In VRAM (`xtx-xt`) the pool
   is 262,144 tokens, shared by every request running. In pinned host RAM (`FREETOKEN_QSA_KV_HOST=1`) it is as large
   as your RAM allows: about a million tokens on the 128 GB reference machine with EXL3 3.05 bpw, three 262k contexts
   with NVFP4.
2. **How far the positions go** sets how long one request can be. The model is trained to 262,144 positions, and a
   longer prompt is refused. `FREETOKEN_ROPE_MAX_POSITION=1048576` extends its rope table to 1,048,576 positions; below
   262,144 the table is the same, so shorter contexts are unchanged.

The two profiles with the K/V in RAM combine them differently:

| Profile | K/V | Pool, all requests together | One request, up to | Positions |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `xtx-xt` | VRAM | 262,144 | 262,144 | native |
| `xtx-xt-4x262k` | host RAM | 1,050,000 (4 x 262,144 and a spare page each) | 262,144 | native |
| `xtx-xt-1m` | host RAM | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000 | extended to 1,048,576 |

- **Several agents that each need the full context**: `xtx-xt-4x262k`. Every request stays within the positions the
  model was trained on.
- **One conversation longer than 262,144 tokens**: `xtx-xt-1m`. Past 262,144 the model runs beyond its trained
  positions: see [Quality](#quality-past-262144-tokens).

Qwen's model card reaches 1M positions with YaRN instead. This build extends the plain rope: it leaves the model as it
is below 262,144 tokens, where YaRN changes its outputs on short texts too, and both kept their retrieval to 988k tokens
([journey.md](journey.md#22-four-conversations-of-262k-or-one-of-1m-the-kv-in-host-ram-2026-10-10)).

Neither profile is agent-validated yet. Both were measured on the reference machine (RX 7900 XTX + RX 7900 XT, MTP head
on), mostly with the EXL3 3.05 bpw checkpoint, on earlier builds than the summary of [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md).

## Running them

```bash
rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt-4x262k --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3-3.05bpw
rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt-1m     --model ~/models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3-3.05bpw
```

Set your client's context window to 262144 (`xtx-xt-4x262k`) or 1000000 (`xtx-xt-1m`). `rdna3/serve.sh --check` says
which pool fits in your RAM.

## What they cost

- **RAM.** The K/V takes 14,144 bytes per token on each card, so 6.9 GiB per 262k conversation on two cards and ~26 GiB
  for 1M tokens, all of it locked. Measured with EXL3 3.05 bpw: ~77 GiB of RAM locked by `xtx-xt-4x262k`, ~75 GiB by
  `xtx-xt-1m`. The NVFP4 checkpoint's experts alone take 63 GiB: on the 126 GiB reference machine three conversations
  fit (`rdna3/serve.sh xtx-xt-4x262k --model DIR -- --kv-reserve-tokens 787500`, 94 GiB locked after the start, ~97 in
  use, with little else running), or two to keep room (`525000`); four, with benchmark tools beside them, ran it out
  of memory. `xtx-xt-1m` is untested with NVFP4. How to count for your machine:
  [limits.md](limits.md#how-much-ram-do-i-need).
- **The RAM tier is off** (`FREETOKEN_HOST_KV=0`): the pool already lives in RAM.
- **Speed.** A request alone decodes a few percent slower than with the K/V in VRAM: at 118k, EXL3 3.05 bpw, 90.6
  tok/s in VRAM, 86.6 on the host with a 262k page table, 84.2 with the 1M one (the kernels read the K/V across PCIe,
  and the wider table costs a few percent more). It reads prompts a little faster: the VRAM the K/V no longer takes goes to
  the expert cache (~11.3k experts per card instead of 9.8k on `xtx-xt`, earlier builds).
- **Prefill goes first.** While a long prompt is read, the other requests barely decode: a 498k-token request decoded
  at 6.3 tok/s while a 237k-token one was read. That is upstream's scheduling, the same on every profile.
  `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE=8` with `FREETOKEN_DECODE_INTERLEAVE_LONG=1` gives the decoding requests eight steps
  after each 16k-token chunk of a long read, at ~3 % of the read's speed, without touching agent turns
  ([options.md](options.md#scheduling)).

## `xtx-xt-4x262k`: four conversations of 262,144 tokens

`rdna3/serve.sh` passes a profile's `CTX` as the cap of one request (`--max-seq-len-override`) and its `KV_TOKENS` as the
pool (`--kv-reserve-tokens`; `CTX` when unset). A request is admitted when the pool can take its prompt plus its
`max_tokens`, which the server lowers to what is left under the cap, so no request reserves more than 262,144 tokens
and four of them fit. On `xtx-xt` the pool is one context, and the conversations that leave it go to the RAM tier.

Four conversations on distinct Python stdlib contexts (no shared prefix, planted values to retrieve), EXL3 3.05 bpw,
an earlier build on which three and four requests did not verify drafts yet:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| 4 cold prompts of 255.7-257.9k tokens sent together | read one after another: 1,027,138 tokens in 463 s (2218 tok/s), every answer right |
| 4 next turns together (257-260k, ~800 new tokens each) | first token after 3.0-4.2 s, decode 29.4-30.1 tok/s each |
| 2 next turns together (259-261k) | first token 1.8-2.9 s, decode 57.2 and 60.6 tok/s |
| 1 next turn alone (261k) | first token 1.8 s, decode 91.3 tok/s (94.1 on `xtx-xt` at 237k, K/V in VRAM) |
| 4 turns together to the cap | each conversation ends at exactly 262,144 tokens (1,048,576 in the pool at once), no error |
| 1 more turn | refused at once: `prompt is too long: 262188 tokens > 262144 maximum` (`context_length_exceeded`) |
| Peaks | 7900 XTX 23.24 of 23.98 GiB, 7900 XT 17.10 of 19.98 GiB; 77.1 GiB of RAM locked, 31.9 GiB left available |

The same four on a later build (one pass): the same scores, the cold reads in 445 s, 29.6-31.6 tok/s each decoding
together, 95.1 alone at 259k. Three and four requests now verify drafts, 2 rows each: +6-9 % at three, +3-6 % at four
greedy, -0.3 to +2.5 % at T 0.6 (a 300k-token pool, 768-token answers:
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#several-requests-and-agents-at-once-xtx-xt)).

One request, EXL3 3.05 bpw (`rdna3/bench/depth_sweep.py`, greedy, one pass): decode 107-110 tok/s at 25-60k tokens and 101 at 248k;
reading a new block 2340-2430 tok/s at 25-60k and 2020 at 248k. An agent turn of 142-360 tokens takes 0.46-0.59 s to
its first token at 224k. NVFP4 with three contexts: 130-340-token turns at 25k 0.58-0.70 s, a 259,728-token prompt
read in 120 s. `--hybrid` brings no clear gain here: the same sweep -8 % at 8.8k, +3 % at 60k and 123k, within 2 %
elsewhere; four agents at ~257k 28.6-30.3 tok/s each against 28.2-30.2 without it ([cpu-experts.md](cpu-experts.md)).

## `xtx-xt-1m`: one conversation of up to 1M tokens

EXL3 3.05 bpw, cold reads of stdlib code with nothing shared, then a 700-token greedy answer:

| Context | Prompt reading | Decode | `xtx-xt` (K/V in VRAM, 250k context) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 118k | 2376 tok/s | 84.2 tok/s | 2185 / 90.6 tok/s |
| 237k | - | 88.5 tok/s | 2128 / 94.1 tok/s |
| 498k | 2014 tok/s | 93.0 tok/s | - |
| 988k | 1780 tok/s (9.3 min) | 84.7 tok/s | - |

The rows come from successive builds: the 498k and 988k ones have both decode fixes of
[journey.md](journey.md#22-four-conversations-of-262k-or-one-of-1m-the-kv-in-host-ram-2026-10-10) (the non-coherent host
memory and the indexer's split top-k), the 118k and 237k decode only the first, the 118k read neither. The 7900 XTX
peaked at 23.20 of 23.98 GiB (sysfs, desktop included) during a 1M read.

An agent conversation on a 498k-token context: first turn 245 s, the next two 4.2 and 2.3 s to the first token (the
prefix is reused). The pool is shared: up to four requests run at once, together within 1M tokens.

### Quality past 262,144 tokens

- **Retrieval** (Python stdlib files with their default values replaced by random ones, so that memory cannot answer,
  plus notes inserted between files; one request asking every question): 100 % from 29k to 988k tokens.
- **A harder set at 988k** (30 code questions, 6 notes, 3 two-hop notes that point to another): 32 of 36. The three
  two-hop questions fail, the answer quoting the pointer note. With the indexer's budget doubled to 4096 (a config
  edit) the same four miss (read at 1551 tok/s, decode 75.5): the sparse attention's selection is not the cause.
- **Next-token loss** on a 988k-token text (this repository's code and docs): 0.46-0.79 nats per token at every depth,
  with no rise past 262k.

## How the K/V lives in RAM

- **The slab** is pinned, device-mapped host memory handed to torch as a GPU tensor (`kernel/host_mapped.py`). The
  decode and verify kernels read the ~2051 tokens each row selects in place, across PCIe. On ROCm it is allocated
  non-coherent, so the GPU's L2 can keep the lines the verify rows of a request share (90 % of their tokens): 2.4x
  faster in the attention kernel, but only 0-2.4 % in serving, where the MoE weights going through the same L2
  probably evict them (not measured). The index tiers stay in VRAM.
- **A prefill** first copies to a VRAM buffer the K/V rows its tokens select, one layer at a time
  (`FREETOKEN_QSA_STAGE_SELECTED`, 28 GB/s), instead of reading each row across PCIe.
- **The answers are bit-identical** to the K/V in VRAM (the same text at 29k and 118k).
- **At 1M tokens** the indexer's page table is 250,000 block columns wide; its top-k reduces it in levels (53 / 64 /
  96 us a layer for 1 / 4 / 8 rows at 988k, on the 7900 XT).

How it was built, what was tried and dropped, and a decode step of `xtx-xt-4x262k` traced kernel by kernel:
[journey.md](journey.md#22-four-conversations-of-262k-or-one-of-1m-the-kv-in-host-ram-2026-10-10) and
[journey.md](journey.md#25-a-decode-step-kernel-by-kernel-2026-10-11-and-12).


---

<!-- file: docs/rdna3/cpu-experts.md -->

# Expert misses computed on the CPU (`--hybrid`)

Off by default, not agent-validated. Measured on a Threadripper 3970X (32 Zen 2 cores, AVX2, 4 x 32 GB DDR4-3200,
STREAM read 72-74 GB/s) with an RX 7900 XTX + 7900 XT on PCIe 4.0 x16.

With `--moe-strategy offload` (every profile), the experts live in RAM and the free VRAM is a cache of them; an expert
a token routes to that is not in the cache (a miss) is copied over PCIe first (26-28 GB/s). Upstream's `hybrid`
strategy computes part of each step's misses on the CPU instead, straight from the RAM banks: only the token's
activation crosses PCIe, the weights do not. Each MoE layer of a decode step then splits its misses: some are fetched
into the cache as before, the rest go to a pool of pinned CPU threads that runs while the GPU computes the hits.

## When it helps

Decode tok/s, MTP head on, the fetch fractions `rdna3/serve.sh --hybrid` sets ([below](#using-it)). One request:
median of 12 sampled 512-token answers (6 prompts x 2, as in
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#how-the-numbers-are-taken)), the `offload` column the benchmark's cell on the same code.
4 at once: 3 rounds of 4 sampled answers, both columns in the same session. Measured on an earlier build than the
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md#summary) summary and not re-measured: compare the two columns with each other, not
with the summary.

| Checkpoint, profile | `offload` | `--hybrid` |
|---|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 `xtx`, one request | 42.7 | **62.3 (+46 %)** |
| NVFP4 `xt`, one request | 34.6 | **52.1 (+51 %)** |
| NVFP4 `xtx-xt`, one request | 82.9 | 84.5 (+2 %) |
| NVFP4 `xtx-xt`, 4 at once | 25.2 each, 92-100 in total | **28.9 each (+15 %), 89-114 in total** |
| EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx`, one request | 54.8 | 57.8 (+5 %) |
| EXL3 3.05 bpw `xtx-xt`, one request | 88.9 | 89.1 (0 %) |

The two-card one-request differences are within the spread of sampled answers: a sampled answer's speed depends on its
text, which changes with the split (the answers of one run spread over +-13 tok/s). The first round of 4 is the
slowest in both columns (92.0 and 89.0 tok/s in total).

**EXL3** gains less. Decoding the trellis is compute-bound on the CPU (~3 G weights/s per thread, about half that per
thread with every core busy) where NVFP4 is bound by the RAM (~120 G weights/s on the whole CPU), and an EXL3 expert is
a third smaller than an NVFP4 one, so its misses cost less to copy. On two cards few of its experts miss: with
`offload`, 1.0-1.4 experts per layer at one request (4.5-6 % of the active ones) and 2.2-2.5 at 4 (`FT_STATS_EVERY` +
`FT_MOE_STATS`); the hybrid split gives the CPU 0.3-0.9 of them, which bounds the gain to a few percent, about what the
hybrid path still costs. Alone on the CPU, a cold expert of rank 0's 384-row slice takes 61 us on 15 threads (54 on
19), against ~42 us to copy it (1.1 MB at the 26-28 GB/s measured for PCIe, estimated): slower, but it runs alongside
the copies; the miss rate is the limit. On `xtx-xt-4x262k` (EXL3 3.05 bpw, measured on an older build than the table
above) `--hybrid` does not pay: one request / 4 at once 82.6 / 34.2 tok/s against 85.9 / 34.2 with `offload`. With every
miss fetched (the CPU idle) the hybrid path is still 2-4 % slower than `offload` there (82.8 / 33.1 against 85.8 /
33.9; measured with the step-number handshake, not with the current task word), and giving the CPU 40 % of the misses
does not win it back (82.5 / 33.3).

**NVFP4 with the K/V in RAM**: `xtx-xt-4x262k` with `--kv-reserve-tokens 787500` (3 x 262k), 20k-token conversations
decoding together, the decode step's period over five 300-step windows (`FT_STATS_EVERY` + `FT_MOE_STATS`; MTP head
on, no drafts at three or more with `FREETOKEN_SPEC_BS_MAX=2` then):

| Requests at once | `offload` | `--hybrid` (the CPU takes 1.8-2.8 of 2.7-4.4 misses a layer) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 3 | 26.1-28.8 ms (32.1-36.4 tok/s each) | 28.1-29.4 ms (31.9-35.3) |
| 4 | 31.5-35.4 ms (29.1-29.8) | 32.9-34.4 ms (29.5-30.0) |

Neither better nor worse within the windows' spread (-4 to +8 %): the +15 % of four requests on `xtx-xt` (K/V in VRAM)
does not carry over to this profile (why was not measured; the K/V's reads cross the same host memory).

## Using it

`rdna3/serve.sh <profile> --hybrid` passes `--moe-strategy hybrid` and the share of each step's misses fetched
(`FREETOKEN_HYBRID_FETCH_FRACTION`, [options.md](options.md)) measured best here: with NVFP4 a quarter on one card (what
`ft bench bw` picks on this machine) and 40 % on two, 60 % with EXL3 (`ft bench bw` does not bench EXL3). With EXL3
on two cards it prints a note: measured even to 2-4 % slower than without.

How the fractions were chosen (decode tok/s; measured on older builds than the first table):

- NVFP4 `xtx`, one request: 15 / 25 / 35 % fetched gave 51.9 / 53.2-54.2 / 50.1 tok/s.
- NVFP4 `xtx-xt`: 25 / 40 / 55 % fetched gave 78.3 / 82.6-82.7 / 78.6 tok/s for one request and 28.6 / 28.6 / 26.9
  each with 4. Why two cards want a larger share fetched, a likely reason, not measured: each rank's pool has half the
  cores and of the RAM's bandwidth but its own PCIe link.
- EXL3 `xtx`, one request (`offload` 49.6): fetch 0.6 / 0.75 gave 51.7 / 50.1; without the hybrid layer's kernels
  ([below](#how-it-works-on-this-hardware)), 0.4 / 0.25 gave 50.1 / 47.0.
- EXL3 `xtx-xt-4x262k`, 4 at once (`offload` 33.9 each): fetch 0.6 gave 31.5; without the hybrid layer's kernels, 0.6
  / 0.4 gave 30.3 / 28.2.
- Every miss on the CPU (`--moe-hybrid-max-fetch 0`; NVFP4 `xtx`, the first working version): the cache stops
  learning, 29.2 tok/s against 39.4 with `offload` and 51.7 with the split `ft bench bw` picks (24.7 % fetched).
- Fetch caps instead of a fraction (`--moe-hybrid-max-fetch` 2 / 4; NVFP4 `xtx-xt`, 4 at once, the first working
  version): 26.3 / 25.1 each, against 27.0 with the `ft bench bw` split and 24.4 with `offload`.

## Costs and caveats

- **The CPU.** The pool spins on its cores while a decode runs and parks 50 ms after the last layer: with `--hybrid`
  on one card, 31 of the 32 cores are busy during generation (15 + 1 per card on two).
- **Other answers than `offload`.** Greedy answers are not bit-identical to offload (the CPU sums in fp32 in another
  order): on `xtx`, 8 of 14 identical, the others diverge after 150-720 characters, all sensible. They are not less
  precise: against an fp64 reference at the model's sizes, one MoE output computed on the CPU is off by 2.3e-3
  (relative), on the GPU by 3.9e-3 (bf16 between its steps), split between them by 3.3-4.0e-3
  ([journey.md](journey.md#27-agent-turns-short-prefills-through-the-expert-cache-2026-10-14)).
- **Answers that move with the expert cache.** Prefill chunks of up to 1280 tokens (agent turns) read their routed
  experts through the cache here too (`FREETOKEN_PREFILL_CACHED_MAX`), which moves the answers as the cache's contents
  do. Time to the first token of a 132-337-token turn at 25k, that path off -> on: NVFP4 `xtx-xt` 1.19-1.24 -> 0.78-0.89
  s, EXL3 3.05 `xtx` 1.50-1.52 -> 1.05-1.18, NVFP4 `xtx` 2.32-2.34 -> 1.63-1.80.
- **Not reproducible.** Two runs of one image (`xtx`, NVFP4, the same settings, greedy) gave the same answers on only 7
  of 14 prompts: `--hybrid` is not reproducible from one run to the next (the cause was not looked for).
- **Long prompts** read at the usual speed (a long prefill streams whole layers to the GPU, as without `--hybrid`): a
  118k-token prompt in 83 s on `xtx`, 61 s on `xtx-xt`, and 9/9 planted questions answered on both.

## How it works on this hardware

- **The GPU <-> CPU handshake.** Upstream's executor signals the CPU pool with stream memory operations. HIP's own
  `hipStreamWriteValue64` / `hipStreamWaitValue64` work, in captured graphs too, on ROCm 10.1 (the PLE disk reads rely
  on them too), and upstream's executor has a HIP backend for them. The hybrid layer's kernels below carry the
  handshake themselves.
- **MTP verify rows.** A verify step runs up to `FREETOKEN_SPEC_VERIFY_M` rows per request. The executor's row bound
  counts them, sized up front, and a larger task is refused; sized for `max(--max-running-requests,
  --cuda-graph-max-bs)` rows only, the C++ scratch grew on the first verify step, in the middle of serving (the EXL3
  scratch below has no such path).
- **Two cards.** Upstream refuses CPU decode with NVFP4 experts under tensor parallelism. Here each rank's executor
  reads its own slices of the banks and its partial joins the GPU partial before the all-reduce, like the GPU path.
  Each rank pins a contiguous half of the cores (without it, both ranks' pools took every physical core).
- **The hybrid layer's fixed cost.** As ported, each MoE layer of a hybrid step added ~12 small graph nodes (a clone of
  the routing, masks, two `where`, a clamp, three device-to-host copies, three stream memops, the copy back and an
  add); a node of a captured graph costs ~3.2 us here, a memop as much as a tiny kernel. On two cards, where one layer
  of a one-request step lasts ~270 us, that cost ~9 % at one request whatever share of the misses the CPU took. What
  this tree does instead:
  - one kernel writes the CPU's inputs straight into its pinned IO rows (a device view of them), another adds the
    CPU's partial back from them; the routing split runs in upstream's hybrid ensure kernel;
  - the two kernels carry the handshake (`FREETOKEN_HYBRID_FLAG_IN_KERNEL`, on) over two pinned words the coordinator
    polls beside upstream's doorbell, with its protocol: the first resets `done` and raises `ready` to the step's task
    word (layer, rows) with system-scope releases, or sets `done` at once when no route goes to the CPU; the
    coordinator takes the task and sets `done`; the second spins on `done` with a system-scope atomic; no stream memop
    is left. The spin needs the atomic: in a bounded test a `volatile` load returned in 0.03 us a poll, too fast to
    reach host memory, and never saw the CPU's store (it hung the server); the atomic took 1.46 us a poll and saw it;
  - the kernel that picks which misses to fetch reads the routes with vector loads and tells the slots used this step
    apart by their usage stamp, where upstream's reads them one dependent scalar load at a time and compares the whole
    cache per route: the same decisions (state compared after every call at the profiles' cache sizes, synthetic Zipf
    routing) in 11.5-19.4 us a layer instead of 17.3-30.4 at 4 rows (159 -> 31 us at 16 rows and an 11k-slot cache);
    it writes the slots apart, so the routing needs no copy;
  - a step that leaves the CPU no route rings nothing (the publish kernel sets `done` itself; upstream's coordinator
    also answers such a doorbell with zeros without waking its pool).

  Measured with the step-number handshake these kernels used before the task word (the task word was not measured):
  EXL3 `xtx-xt-4x262k` with every miss fetched (the CPU gets nothing), against offload 85.8 / 33.9 tok/s: 80.3 / 31.6
  without the last three of these changes, 82.8 / 33.1 with them; NVFP4 `xtx-xt`, one request: 71.0 (first version),
  74.3 (the hybrid layer's kernels), 78.3 (all).
- **The GPU skips the CPU's routes** (`FREETOKEN_HYBRID_SKIP_CPU_ROUTES`, on). The NVFP4 and EXL3 decode kernels run
  one program per route; with the skip off they read no "inactive" slot, so a route the CPU takes goes to the GPU as
  slot 0 at weight 0 and is computed in full (for EXL3 a whole trellis decode). With it they write zeros for a slot of
  -1 without a read; the EXL3 rotation and scale kernels read slot 0's scales for it (weight 0). +1-3 %
  ([the table below](#levers-measured)).
- **Rows routed to the same expert.** Computed one (row, expert) route at a time, an expert two rows of a step use
  (MTP verify rows, several requests) is read from RAM, or for EXL3 decoded, once per row: 8-13 % of the CPU's routes
  in these runs (`FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_ROUTE_STATS=n` prints the share). NVFP4: one task per (expert, row block) runs its
  routes back to back, the second from the core's cache (`FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_GROUP`); EXL3: each tile row is decoded
  once for all of them. Both bit-identical to one route at a time.
- **EXL3 experts** have no CPU path upstream. The executor reads the EXL3 banks in place (mul1 codebook, 2-4 bits):
  rotate in (`H(x * suh)`), the gate|up products, silu and the rotation into down's domain, the down products, the
  rotation out and the routed sum, AVX2 + F16C. The trellis states are decoded 8 at a time from one 64-bit window, the
  bytesum of `s * 0x83DCD12D` through `vpmaddubsw` / `vpmaddwd`, and the GEMV accumulates `x * bytesum` and adds the
  affine part of mul1 once per column (no per-weight fp16 rounding: relative error ~1.7e-3 on a layer's output with
  bf16 in and out, `tests/moe/test_cpu_moe_exl3.py`). The tiles of a column are 7.7 KB apart and come cold from RAM in
  serving: software prefetch 6 rows ahead takes a cold expert from 307 to 95 us, and the group plan as compile-time
  constants the executor's time per route from 104 to 44-48 us warm (31 threads), against ~66 us to copy one over PCIe
  (the cold time was measured before that last change).

## Levers measured

Each lever behind a switch, every arm bit-identical (greedy answers 14/14 between the first and the last arm of each
profile, as long as the expert cache got the same size: it follows the free VRAM at start, and on the 7900 XTX the
desktop's share moves it by a few slots, which changes the evictions and so the texts). Decode tok/s, 12 sampled
answers (their texts differ from run to run: the sampler is exact only up to fp32 atomic order, so they compare as
means, ~2 % run to run) and two greedy 1024-token answers (same texts across arms); measured on an older build than the
first table.

| Lever | NVFP4 `xtx-xt` (fetch 0.4) | NVFP4 `xtx` (0.25) | EXL3 `xtx` (0.6) | EXL3 `xtx-xt-4x262k` (0.6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | 80.1, 28.3 each with 4 | 54.0 | 52.5 | 83.3, 34.3 |
| the GPU skips the CPU's routes (kept, on) | **82.6 (+3 %), 28.9 (+2 %)**; greedy +2 / +7 % | **54.5 (+1 %)**; greedy +2 / +3 % | **53.0 (+1 %)**; greedy +2 / +4 % | 82.6, 34.2 |
| + cores by slice size | 82.3, 28.9 | - | - | 82.3, 33.6 |
| + SMT siblings | 53.4, 16.3 | 46.5 (with the skip only) | - | 61.5, 23.5 |
| the skip + EXL3 column blocks of 4 | - | - | 54.0; greedy +2 / 0 % against the skip alone | - |
| `offload` | 78.2 (another session), 24.4 | 39.4 (another session) | 50.0 | 85.9, 34.2 |

- **Cores by slice size** (`FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_CORES_BY_SLICE`, off): the ranks' slices are uneven (NVFP4 352 / 288
  rows at 0.55, EXL3 384 / 256: its 128-row Hadamard blocks round 0.55 to 0.6), so rank 0 has ~22 % (NVFP4) and 50 %
  (EXL3) more CPU work per core; the pools can split 18 / 14 and 19 / 13 cores instead (checked in the logs). No gain:
  the CPU is not what the step waits for at these miss rates ([When it helps](#when-it-helps)).
- **SMT** (`FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_SMT`, off): the pool also on the worker cores' SMT siblings. Alone on the CPU it takes a
  cold EXL3 expert 5-11 % faster (16 cores, 15 -> 30 threads: 62.6-64.0 -> 55.7-56.0 us; 3 runs); in serving it costs
  14-42 % (the spinning workers then share every core with the server's own threads; not measured further).
- **EXL3 column blocks** (`FREETOKEN_CPU_MOE_EXL3_COLS`, 1): a task takes n adjacent tile columns, the first
  prefetching their contiguous row segments. Alone on the CPU (8 cold experts per task, 2 runs): 31 threads, slice 640,
  71 -> 64-66 us a route with 4 or 8; with 15-19 threads no gain (8: a loss). In serving on `xtx` within the noise
  (54.0 against 53.0), so it stays at 1.

  the engine this repository modifies (expert offload, radix and hybrid caches, FTW format, APIs, the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
  model code, the exact sampling kernels whose barrier-free draw this build uses on ROCm).
- **zihaomu**: FreeToken's ROCm support pull requests
  [#133](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken/pull/133), [#134](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken/pull/134)
  and [#135](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken/pull/135) (HIP-portable JIT kernels, CUDA-only backends gated
  off, RCCL for tensor parallelism), included as they were proposed.
- **lukascechovic** ([lukascechovic/FreeToken](https://github.com/lukascechovic/FreeToken), branch `rocm-gfx1201`, a
  community ROCm port of FreeToken): the LDS budget clamp for RDNA's 64 KiB, the TP>1 relay
  handshake, the GDN boundary carry across prefill chunks, the first qwen4_exp tensor-parallel port that this one was
  rewritten from, and the `Dockerfile.gfx1201` (in that port) that `Dockerfile.rdna3` derives from.
- **flash-linear-attention**, vendored under `python/freetoken/kernel/fla` as upstream does.
- **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next** by the Qwen team and its NVFP4 checkpoint by RadixArk; their licenses apply to the weights.
- **exllamav3** by turboderp ([turboderp-org/exllamav3](https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3), MIT License): the
  EXL3 format and its checkpoints (e.g. turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3). The reference codec and the RDNA3 kernels
  here are written from its format description and CUDA sources (bit layout, codebooks, tile order, n-gram rings); no
  exllamav3 code runs in this build.

Original to this repository: the uneven tensor-parallel split and unequal-card planning, weight-only int8 dense layers
and their GEMVs, the split-K bf16 GEMVs, the host-memory all-reduce, the top-k-first sampler and the sorted-threshold
sampling path for ROCm, rank-0 token broadcast, the tuned NVFP4 tiles, the blocked PLE and prefill MoE paths, expert
reuse in prefill on ROCm, batch-invariant multi-request decoding, the RAM tier for conversations, the MTP-head speculative decoding for
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the attention K/V in host RAM for long contexts, short prefills through the expert cache with the
next layer's experts predicted, the tokenizer's prompt prefix cache, the EXL3 reader and its RDNA3 kernels, the profiles and tooling, and the measurements in these docs.
